en: Now begins the twelfth chapter:
"O sinless one, you have indeed declared this entire dharma of the four social orders;
now tell us truly the supreme result that arises from actions."

The first half-verse is intended to show the completion of the treatise’s subject matter (*śāstrārtha*) in order to eliminate any further expectation [of more]. The inclusion of the word "entire" (*kṛtsna*) is for the sake of honor. It indicates that within this treatise, all these duties prescribed by the Smṛti have been taught, including those pertaining to the secret [Upanishadic] portions. By means of the disciple, the teacher’s own total accomplishment of the treatise is set forth; however, this is not intended as a literal statement. Here, one should not understand the relationship of disciple and teacher as a factual reality. The author himself divides the work in this manner. Furthermore, the word *dharma*, which denotes what ought to be done, reiterates the collection of injunctions and prohibitions. Therefore, since the connection between action and its fruit has not yet been stated, it is explained hereafter. When it is said, "The entire *dharma* has been declared by you," the statement is appropriate with respect to the injunctions and prohibitions.

Furthermore, for which action is the connection with its fruit intended to be investigated, such that it is said: "one should declare the production of the fruits of actions"? For as many obligatory (*nitya*) rites as there are, they are performed simply because they are enjoined by the scriptures; their fruit is not to be aimed at, since they do not have a fruit as their purpose. As for those optional (*anitya*) rites, in almost every case their fruits have already been stated, such as: "The giver of water attains satisfaction" (MDh 4.230), and "Heaven and long life" (ĀpDh 1.5.15), and so forth. Even where one might think a fruit has not been mentioned, heaven and the like have indeed been established [as the result]. Those purificatory rites (*saṃskārakarma*), such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) and others, possess their fruit solely through the fruit of the action pertaining to the specific object to be purified; they do not require an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) result. Furthermore, those occasional rites (*naimittika*) such as the purification of substances and bathing upon touching a *caṇḍāla* also have only visible purposes. Indeed, they are performed for the sake of purification, because engagement in worldly transactions is prohibited for those who are impure. And the penances (*prāyaścitta*) have the very purposes just mentioned immediately following them. Therefore, we do not know for which of these actions the fruit is intended to be investigated.

Regarding prohibitions: because they themselves will be discussed later in passages such as, "By the defects of action born of the body" (MDh 12.9), the performance of those very prohibitions is likewise enjoined by the scripture. Now, an objection may be raised: if there were a desire for a fruit, the entitlement would not apply to all subjects; rather, only one who possesses that desire would be entitled.

It is said: here no such result is specified as one that is desired; rather, the perception of an undesirable result is presented here. That [undesirable result] is certainly not desired, nor does anyone wish for the attainment of what is undesirable. Therefore, the status of being the object of all [actions] is established. As for the statement, "The scripture enjoins the performance of prohibitions," this is saying too little; it is not merely that the performance is carried out there in that manner, but rather everything enjoined by the scripture is performed.

However, that scripture establishes the duty [of certain acts] for someone seeking a specific result, while for others it does so as a contingent act (*naimittika*) even without a result. But here, since there is no scriptural mention of a contingency such as "as long as one lives," for what purpose is the prohibited act not performed?
Furthermore, demerit (*pratyavāya*) is seen to follow from indifference: "By the desire to kill a Brahmin, one falls into hell" (MDh 11.205).

But surely, that which is prohibited, such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa and so forth, is not enjoined by the scripture (*śāstra*). For it is only that which is enjoined by the scripture that is logically connected with a scriptural result, as in the case of the injunction: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice. Indeed, the understanding that a sacrifice is to be performed arises from the scripture and not from any other source. In this case, however, the worldly engagement [in prohibited acts] due to hatred and the like is non-scriptural (*aśāstrīya*). And it is not proper for that which is non-scriptural to be connected with a scriptural result. As for what was said—that "neglect is shown to entail demerit" (*pratyavāya*)—what is the expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) here? Since the understanding arises from the scripture that "one who acts toward one who hates [him] must not do so," the meaning of the sentence is complete. What word is there here that would require further expectation?

To analyze this in detail would entail a vast expansion of the text; however, this is the summary: In the prohibitive injunction “One should not harm living beings,” the object of the prohibition (*pratiṣedha-bhāvārtha*) is the act of harming. It is heard [in grammar] that there is a relationship between the agent and the instrument. In that context, the injunction first has a requirement for the subject to be enjoined (*niyojya-viṣayākāṅkṣā*). There, the understanding of the person to be enjoined arises as follows: “This must not be done by me. The purpose is not merely the enjoining of an action, because an injunction consists in the enjoining of a person. And here, that person to be enjoined is presented through the teaching of the nature of harming—which, in common worldly usage, is an activity characterized by aversion—and which proceeds toward its object by way of that aversion. One who proceeds toward killing by his own will is the one who “should kill”; yet he is not fit to be the subject of this injunction, for he is already the object of the prohibition. Furthermore, the connection of the injunction with its own object does not occur through the person being a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), since the object of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is already established elsewhere. Nor does the person to be enjoined realize his status as a subject of the injunction merely by being a recipient of instruction; rather, he does so only when he determines that the prohibited object has an undesirable result. Such is the worldly understanding: when one says, “A finger should be given to the court official,” it is understood that the performance of that [prohibited act] is a cause of misfortune due to the transgression of the prohibition. And it is not appropriate to discard this worldly understanding and propose another reason. In that case, even if the undesirable result is not explicitly heard, it is proper to infer it from the force of the prohibition; how much more so where it is actually heard? For it is not right to abandon what is explicitly stated in scripture. Nor can it be argued that the mention of results such as hell is merely an indicator of the discussion, because according to the aforementioned logic, the connection with a result is established through the very expectation of a result inherent in the injunction itself.

Furthermore, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) serve as supplements to injunctions (*vidhi*). However, no injunction is heard here, nor is one provided by context, because it is precisely the connection between action and its fruit that is intended to be established as the primary subject. Indeed, actions are not enjoined here; rather, their connection with the fruit is stated. Nor do these hundreds of sentences thereby become purposeless; let them be, for this perspective may well serve as a basis for the author of the *Smṛti*. For otherwise, these sentences could not be explained at all. Herein, there exists nothing that is not a supplement to an injunction.

If it be argued that this explanation is merely figurative praise (*guṇavāda*) and thus represents even the authors of the scriptures as being mistaken, we say no; for those who speak thus do not show contempt for the great seers (*maharṣis*) by way of exaggeration. "Agham" means sin or evil. "Anagha" is an address intended as praise on account of his stainlessness. "Śaṃsa" refers to one who is restrained in speech. (12.1)
That righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Hear the definitive conclusion regarding this entire yoga of action. (12.2)

This is the answer to what was asked: "Listen to that which I have been asked. The connection is with the phrase "the application of action" (karmaṇo yogam). And since that [application] is the subject under discussion, it should be understood as being in relation to the fruit alone. 12.2.
Action, arising from mind, speech, and body, bears fruit that is auspicious or inauspicious;
the destinies of men—whether superior, inferior, or middling—are born of action.

The mention of "the auspicious" is by way of illustration; or rather, it is for the purpose of prescribing the activity of mind and speech, since action (*karman*) arises from the mind, from speech, and from the body. The word "action" does not refer solely to bodily movement in the sense of ritual sacrifice (*ijyā*); what then? It refers to every kind of activity (*kriyā*), even that consisting of yoga and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). The word "fruit" (*phala*) is connected with each [of the preceding terms]: the fruit of the auspicious and the fruit of the inauspicious. One should not understand it thus: that the attainment of the auspicious and inauspicious fruits results only from the performance of action accomplished through bodily activity. Rather, it is exactly the same when arising from mind, speech, and body. Therefore, the attainment of fruit is ordained from this threefold action. (12.3)
One should know that for this embodied being—whether characterized by these three types, having these three bases, or endowed with the ten marks—it is the mind that is the instigator. (12.4)

But surely, [acts such as] "one should sacrifice with those possessing staffs" and "one should not harm" are both auspicious and inauspicious; all of these are accomplished through bodily activity. Through giving (*dāna*), there is the cessation of one's own ownership and the production of ownership in another, and that was previously enjoined by the rule "with the right hand," and so forth. Sacrifice (*yajña*) as well, being of the nature of a ritual performance ending with the final bath (*avabhṛtha*), is brought to completion through bodily activity. Likewise, the punishment of a group (*saṃghāta-daṇḍa*) and the like are well known to be physical. In that case, what action is there that can arise from the mind?

Therefore, he says: one should know that the mind is the initiator of this object. For all the activities of the mind—such as seeing and so forth—do not occur when these three [the eye, etc. are absent; nor does a material activity [occur]. For instance, first of all, one perceives this object with the mind: "This is exactly such-and-such," or "This is the cause of pleasure or pain for that thing. Then, depending on that, [one wonders], "How can this be accomplished by the mind? Thereafter, one resolves: "I shall accomplish this from here, and not that. In that regard, when action is primary, there is bodily movement and verbal expression. Therefore, the mind is the initiator of everything, like one who acts preceded by a command.

However, in the case of what is not preceded by conscious intent (*abuddhipūrva*), the prior perception of a form as being of such-and-such a nature is not necessarily required—such as, for example, acting with the notion that it is a refreshing drink because its color resembles wine; or, due to the occurrence of dense darkness, acting toward another's wife [with that same notion]; or other instances occurring by chance, such as the killing of living beings like mosquitoes through the movement of the hands or turning over on one's side while asleep—even in those cases, agency has been established as the basis for engaging in penances.

It is of three kinds, through the distinction of speech, mind, and body as the means; it has three bases, through the distinction of the superior, inferior, and middling destinies. The mental and bodily actions are each of three kinds, while those consisting of speech are of four kinds. These are the ten characteristics. He will explain them further below. (12.4)
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind, and adherence to falsehood—these are the three kinds of mental action. (12.5)

Covetousness (*abhidhyāna*) is the constant contemplation of surpassing another's property with a mind of envy regarding that object, thinking: "How much wealth of horses and cattle he has! How many goats and sheep! What abundance of horses! Woe to fate! Why does he have such prosperity? Now, how might I take this away from him? Or rather, it would be better if he did not possess this.
Others, however, say that it is the thought: "I shall completely surpass this wealth."

They connect this with the thought of what is undesirable for another. It refers to contemplating means for the destruction of another, thinking, "If he dies," or "May that [gain] be mine. But has not coveting the property of another already been mentioned? Since that is already established by this very [rule], it would be redundant. For this term is general: whatever is undesirable or unintended for another should not be contemplated. Even the loss of wealth is certainly not desired by another; and out of fear of this, people do not even utter the words "something of another's. They explain "undesirable" as that which is prohibited.
Even in this view, coveting the property of another is intended primarily for its own sake;

likewise is false adherence. This includes taking the meaning of a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) as a final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*), the invalidity of the Vedas, the grasping at non-selfhood, and so forth.
Others, however, say that it refers to hatred toward that which is eternal and free from worldly desires.

And this threefold unwholesome mental activity is the opposite of the wholesome. [The wholesome consists of: lack of covetousness toward the property of others, compassion for all sentient beings, and faith in the existence of dharma and so forth. And thus the Blessed Vyāsa said: "One should reflect with the mind upon these three things: lack of covetousness regarding the wealth of others, friendliness toward all sentient beings, and that there is fruit for those who possess dharma. (12.5)
Harshness, falsehood, slander in every form, and idle chatter—these constitute the fourfold nature of speech. (12.6)
Taking what has not been given, violence contrary to the rules, and adultery with another's wife—this is remembered as the threefold bodily [action]. (12.7)

Because of the primary importance of the scriptures, it is faulty to take from the wicked what has not been given; this applies likewise to the wives of others, such as virgins and so forth. The taking up of contrary qualities consists of protection and restraint of the senses. This is tenfold according to the divisions of mind, speech, and body; through the distinction between wholesome and unwholesome activity, there are twenty types. (12.7)
This person experiences the mental [result] of both good and evil through the mind alone;
the action performed by speech through speech, and that which is physical through the body alone. (12.8)
Some say that one obtains mental suffering from that action by which distress is produced in another.

We, however, maintain that the attainment of mental suffering results from the threefold mental [unwholesome roots] that have been described; the same applies to the two subsequent cases as well. 12.8
Through the defects of actions born of the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being;
through those of speech, to the state of birds or beasts; and through those of the mind, to the status of a low-born caste.

This is intended to indicate a predominance; for the most part, these are the respective causes for these classes of beings, yet this is not an absolute rule. For he will state that even those who have committed great sins wander among the animals (MDh 12.55ff). The mention of birds and wild animals is for the purpose of illustrating the animal kingdom in general. This passage is primarily intended to demonstrate that among the actions of mind, speech, and body, each subsequent one is more serious than the preceding. (12.9)
The restraint of speech, the restraint of mind, and likewise the restraint of body—he in whose intellect these are firmly established is called a "triple-staffed" ascetic (tridaṇḍin). || 12.10 ||

Self-restraint is the staff. Restraint of speech is the non-indulgence in harshness; the same applies to the other two [senses]. He in whose intellect these staffs are established—who does not stumble, thinking "this must not be done by me"—is called a *tridaṇḍin* (one who possesses the triple staff). It is not the ignoble man who merely carries a heavy wooden staff. 12.10.
Having cast aside this triple staff among all living beings and having thoroughly restrained desire and anger, a person then attains perfection.

The collection of the three staffs is *tridaṇḍa*. Because it is seen [in the list] beginning with "vessel" (*pātra*) and because it is stated [by Pāṇini] that such compounds are not feminine (cf. Pāṇ. 2.4.17), it is masculine. Having placed them in the intellect, having fixed them in the mind; or, the state of non-injury toward all beings is established as the *tridaṇḍa* that has been set down. Restraint of desire and anger is excellent. From that, one goes to—that is, attains—perfection called liberation. This introduction is an exposition of the spiritual self (*ādhyātmika*). But whose is this perfection? Or who is the enjoyer of the fruits of modified actions in the hereafter? The body ends in ashes, and we do not perceive anything beyond that. Therefore, wishing to demonstrate the person who is the qualified agent (*adhikārin*) in respect to all merits and demerits, he begins [the discourse]. 12.11.
That which causes this self to act is called the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field);
but that which performs the actions is called the *bhūtātman* (the elemental self) by the wise. || 12.12 ||

He is the self-initiator of the activity of this body, which consists of the vibration of its functions; his agency arises through the power of effort (*prayatna*). He is the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field). The genitive case in the phrase “of this self” (*asyātmanaḥ*) is one of apposition. The word “self” (*ātman*) refers here to the body, because the body also exists for the sake of the [true] Self. That which performs actions characterized by drinking and so forth—the agent called the “body” produced by that [effort]—is called the *bhūtātman* (the elemental self), being a collection of the elements such as earth and the rest, due to its inferiority. The *bhūtātman* is thus the self that is a modification of the elements. Accordingly it has been said: “There are two selves: the inner self (*antarātman*) and the bodily self (*śarīrātman*). (12.12)
There is another inner self, distinct [from the body], known as the *jīva*, which is innate to all embodied beings;
by means of it, one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout successive births. (12.13)

But what indeed is this so-called *jīva*, given that they consider the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) alone to be the *jīva*? For here two things are perceived: the body and the inner self (*antarātman*) who is to be known through the notion of "I. Apart from these, what else could there be called a *jīva*?

Some, first of all, say that the *liṅga*—which is described as being enveloped by the subtle elements beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and which is stated [in Sāṃkhyakārikā 40]: "The *liṅga* transmigrates, devoid of experience, yet permeated by dispositions"—is that by which the status of being an instrument (*itikaraṇatva*) with respect to cognition is established. For that [subtle body] is the substratum of the gross elements, since it alone serves as the substratum for the external elements known as the body. And when the body exists, the self possesses the state of being an experiencer of pleasure and pain. Therefore, it is expressed by the instrumental case-ending as "by which."

Others, however, think as follows: the individual soul (*jīva*) is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), consisting of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṃkāra*). Since it is designated by the term "internal organ," its reference by means of the instrumental case is indeed appropriate.

And the word "inner self" (*antarātman*) is also appropriate because of its identity with that [organ]. Furthermore, the word "innate" (*sahaja*) is used because it is never separated from that [organ] until the attainment of liberation or until the final dissolution. (12.13)
Both of these—the Great Principle (Mahat) and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña)—are joined with the elements;
they remain pervading that which abides within high and low beings.

He who, pervading them, abides within all beings—high and low, manifold, and of various forms; that is, he who remains and takes refuge in them. And for this reason, he is the agent of all actions, since the root *sthā* has multiple meanings.

Who is it that stands pervading these high and low beings? It is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is distinct from the conscious and unconscious world, whose nature is supreme bliss, and which will be explained further on.

"Conjoined with the elements" means the five elements. "The Great One" (*mahān*) is that by which one experiences, as has been stated. "The Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajña*) refers to "this Self" (MDh 12.12).

Even according to the view of pervasion, he is situated as the second [principle]. And his being the "resort" (*saṃśrayaṇa*) is because he is the cause of this entire world; for an effect resorts to its cause, and thus resorting is simply dependence. And so says your honor Vyāsa: "These two persons exist in the world: the perishable and the imperishable."

"The perishable consists of all beings; the immutable is called the unchanging (*kūṭastha*). (BhG 15.16) By the word "perishable" (*kṣara*), all this is denoted, namely the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the moving and the unmoving. The "immutable" (*akṣara*) is the causal primordial nature (*prakṛti*), so called because it does not perish even during dissolution due to its nature as the cause. Alternatively, the "perishable" is the body and the "immutable" is the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). Its "unchangingness" (*kūṭasthatva*) is due to the non-cessation of its status as agent and enjoyer until liberation is attained. But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
He who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them as the imperishable Lord. (BhG 15.17) || 12.14 ||
Innumerable forms issue forth from his body,
which constantly set in motion all beings, both high and low.

By the word *mūrti* (form), whatever material cause-and-effect exists is meant, as well as its power (*śakti*). All this emerges from the body of that Supreme Self (*paramātman*). His very nature is his body; the designation is made with a distinction, as in the expression "the body of a stone statue. They are innumerable and infinite, like waves from the ocean. It is said that they "issue forth" or "manifest. By these manifested powers, this world moves; the meaning is that it becomes active. Since there is no movement without a body, sense organs, and consciousness, it is said that [the powers] "cause it to move."

Others, however, maintain that the primary cause is the body and that the material elements are not [the cause] here, because the body is the body of the Supreme Self and its activity is dependent upon Him. (12.15)
For men who have committed evil deeds, after death, another body certainly arises from the five elements alone for the purpose of undergoing torment. 12.16.

A body distinct from the five elements arises after death. This is what is meant: a body composed of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*) arises even without semen and blood. For evildoers, the body consists of the five elements; however, for those who have performed meritorious deeds, it consists merely of light (*taijasa*) and ether (*ākāśa*). As it has been said: "Having become wind, possessing the form of space" (MDh 2.82). *Yātanā* is an excess of torment. That which is intended for that purpose is that which is extremely firm and capable of enduring supermundane suffering. 12.16.
Having experienced those torments of Yama with this very body,
they dissolve part by part back into those same elemental constituents.

Yama is a specific deity who performs the punishment and other acts against evildoers; the torments seen there belong to him. Having experienced those [torments] with that body composed of the five elements, those bodies dissolve again into those subtle elemental constituents (bhūtamātrā). 12.17.
Having experienced those faults born of attachment to sense objects, which result in future suffering,
he approaches those same two of great splendor, his impurities now dispelled.

From attachment to sense objects, from indulging in forbidden objects, and from that attachment which is forbidden, there arise defects produced by evil; having experienced sufferings in hell through that experience of suffering, one becomes "one whose stains are removed" and "one whose sins are destroyed. Those two [sons] were both of great splendor.

Which two? The Great One (mahat) and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). These two are the primary subjects. Furthermore, by the immediately following verse, it is the Knower of the Field alone who is experienced as the locus of pleasure and pain; and since the pronoun "he" (saḥ) refers back to that very same subject, it would follow [from your interpretation] that he "attains the Knower of the Field. But that is a contradiction: the same entity cannot be both the goal to be attained and the attainer.

True; a figurative distinction is intended here. The meaning of "he approaches" (*abhyeti*) is that he remains as nothing more than this: namely, as the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), which is designated as the "Great One" (*mahat*) consisting of the aggregate of the vital breaths and so forth; in the state of fruition, only that much remains. And the subtle body (*liṅga*) is the living *kṣetrajña*.
Others, however, explain [the two terms] as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Those actions that result in happiness are experienced as pleasant after the evil has been exhausted. When evil stands as an obstacle, even if it is slight, no happiness arises; just as when there is even a slight indigestion, eating does not lead to pleasure. (12.18)
Together with him, those two unweariedly perceive his merit and his evil;
thus joined, he experiences happiness and suffering both in this world and after death. (12.19)
Now, if that [Self] and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) were connected, then in the phrase "of him who sees," to what would the word "his" refer? Some say it refers to the individual soul (jīva);
for it has been stated: "He alone is the Knower of the Field; he alone is the individual soul."

Now, regarding the indicative mark (*liṅga*): but surely that very thing has already been stated by the word "great" (*mahat*). Or rather, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—consisting of the great [intellect] (*mahat*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and so forth—is what is meant.

Even in that case, what is the connection of the inferential mark (liṅga) with merit and demerit? For that [mark] is indeed a subtle form of the elements, as was stated in the passage beginning, "But this [is] of those seven."

Therefore, we consider that what has been explained by others regarding the previous verse [58], namely, that "those two" (*tāv evobhau*) in *MDh* 12.18 are understood to be "the Great One and the Supreme Self" (*mahat-paramātmānau*), is precisely what we regard as correct. For an analogy is applicable to those two: because the Great One, being an instrument (*karaṇa*), is metaphorically designated as the agent (*kartṛ*), just as in the expression "the pieces of wood cook. Furthermore, the distinction in the reference to "his" (*tasya*) is thus appropriately established as referring to the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*).

The statement of the analogy regarding merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which reside in the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) and depend upon the Supreme Self, is for the purpose of making known that the experience of all pleasure and pain is dependent upon that [Supreme Self]. As it has been said:
"Impelled by the Lord, one may go either to heaven or even to the abyss" (Manu Dharma Śāstra 3.22–23). And this impelling is nothing other than the will itself, as regulated by merit and demerit.

But surely, if merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) were to act as restrictors with respect to desire, his sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) would be lost. This has been shown in the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtras]: just as in this world a king bestows rewards according to service, yet his status as a lord does not thereby depart. Therefore, it is designated that "one sees the Great One and the Supreme Self. The word "his" refers to the knowledge of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). That too is incorrect, because it contradicts the subsequent text: "he attains union with Yama. For no contact or connection of anyone with the Supreme Self is ever mentioned; nor indeed is there any connection whatsoever with the Supreme Self.

If that is so, then in this context [verse 62], the phrase "by which two" does not refer to the Great Principle (mahat) and the Self (ātman). What then? It refers to merit (dharma) and demerit (pāpa), since those two are also the subject under discussion. Thus, it means: "He sees those two—merit and demerit."

If the word *mahat* refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the inconsistency is even greater; for the Supreme Self, in its capacity as the Seer, has no dependence upon an instrument. Indeed, the very locus is the nature of the Supreme Self as Consciousness, according to the verse: "He approaches those two alone" (MDh 12.18). Of what sort is this "approaching"? If it is the attainment of that state, it cannot be accomplished merely by the removal of impurities. If, on the other hand, it is an inclination toward attaining that [state], even that does not occur for one who is bodiless once the elements have dissolved.
Therefore, those two see the Dharma as belonging to that very self; this is to be understood as before. 12.19.
If one practices dharma for the most part and unrighteousness only slightly, being enveloped by those very elements, he enjoys happiness in heaven. (12.20)

For the most part, that is, in the majority of cases, one attains happiness in heaven through those very elements, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the gross elements (mahābhūta). || 12.20 ||
But if one mostly practices unrighteousness and righteousness only to a small degree,
abandoned by those elements, he undergoes the torments of Yama.

But has it not been stated that "the body of evildoers arises from the five elements alone" (MDh 12.16)? What, then, is meant by saying they are "abandoned by those elements"? It is replied: the body is not composed of the [ordinary] elements, nor do torments belong to one who is without a body. Rather, those [bodies] are entirely distinct from the human body; these other bodies, which initiate a form soft, smooth, and delicate, are of a completely different nature.
He is said to have renounced for the sake of expiating the assault of suffering; he has renounced those bodies which are to be enjoyed in heaven. 12.21
Having undergone those torments in the Yāmis, that living being, freed from defilement,
returns once again to those very five elements, each according to its own portion.

This has been explained previously; this is the intended meaning of these four verses [69]. If the unrighteousness (*adharma*) is great, then there are the torments of Yama; but not when the unrighteousness is slight, for in that case, heaven is attained through the experience of unhappiness in this very world [69–70]. || 12.22 ||

Having observed these destinies of the living being by means of his own mind— both those resulting from righteousness and those from unrighteousness— one should always fix the mind upon righteousness.

This has a very brief meaning. The phrase "from dharma and adharma" involves the elision of the negative particle (nañ), meaning "due to the cause of dharma and adharma. Of the living being, the knower of the field, the Self—by means of his own mind, through the authority of the scriptures, he should experience that. This is the summary of the fruit of the entire meaning of the scripture. 12.23.
One should know that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are the three qualities (*guṇa*) of the Self, by which the Great One (*mahat*) stands pervading all these states without exception. (12.24)

That which pertains to *dharma* and *adharma* and is useful for the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) has been explained. Now, the section on knowledge (*vidyākāṇḍa*) is commenced. Therein, for the sake of the preliminary exposition (*prakriyā*), a process is set forth that appears to rely upon duality. The three qualities (*guṇa*), beginning with *sattva*, belong to the Self (*ātman*). Here, "Self" does not refer to the individual soul (*jīva*), but rather to the Great One (*mahat*) itself. The word "Self" denotes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and does not denote the state of being the inner subject (*pratyaktva*). For the Puruṣa is indeed devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). Alternatively, they are designated as belonging to the Self—the enjoyer—by virtue of being objects of enjoyment.

And by "the Great" (mahat), the Pradhāna alone is meant, due to proximity. For the first manifestation of transformation belonging to the Pradhāna is called "the Great. Just as one who is living remains amidst various modifications while in the state of being alive, so it is said of this [Pradhāna], because it is the source-nature (prakṛti) of all modifications. || 12.24 ||
Whichever of these qualities is predominant in the body in its entirety at any given time, it then makes that embodied being consist primarily of that quality. (12.25)

Although everything consists of the three *guṇas*, nevertheless, whenever a particular *guṇa*—by virtue of the predominance of past karma—surpasses [the others] in its entirety and reaches a state of preponderance, it then overcomes the other *guṇas* for the person (*puruṣa*). Consequently, the embodied being becomes characterized by that dominant *guṇa*; he manifests only its specific quality and, as it were, abandons the other *guṇas*. (12.25)
Sattva is knowledge, tamas is ignorance, and passion (rajas) is known as attachment and aversion.
This is their pervasive nature, which rests within all beings. 12.26

This is their common characteristic, pervasive among all living beings: knowledge is the faculty of perception; ignorance is delusion (*moha*), which is not merely a state of unconsciousness as in conditions such as intoxication or fainting. Passion (*rajas*) consists of both these forms. By the terms "attachment" (*rāga*) and "aversion" (*dveṣa*), the conjunction of both qualities is expressed. Furthermore, for those under the influence of right knowledge, there is neither excessive anger nor excessive negligence; that is *rajas*. Its nature is its very essence (*vapuḥ-svabhāva*). Because the latent impressions of the seed are not severed, it persists until the attainment of *brahman*. (12.26)
In that state, whatever he perceives within himself as joined with joy, tranquil and radiant as if pure, let him understand that to be *sattva*. (12.27)

A sensation conjoined with joy appears as pure radiance, as if pure, being undefiled by rajas and tamas; it is free from the defects of intoxication, pride, passion, hatred, greed, delusion, fear, sorrow, and envy. All [sensation] is thus. And this state may be experienced through self-awareness at a single moment. (12.27)
But that which is joined with suffering and is disagreeable to oneself, know that to be the quality of passion (rajas), which constantly carries away embodied beings. (12.28)

That which is conjoined with suffering and fragmented is not of the nature of pure joy; therefore, it is said to be "displeasing" because it is permeated by suffering and is not united with joy. It is "contrary" (apratipa), meaning indirect or not manifest, being ultimate in nature. This is the form of *rajas*; its meaning is that it impels one toward sense objects and generates longing. (12.28)
But that which is joined with delusion, unmanifest, consisting of sense-objects, beyond reasoning, and unknowable—one should understand that to be *tamas*. (12.29)

Delusion (*moha*) is instability, the absence of discrimination between what is appropriate and what is inappropriate. Its object (*viṣaya*) is the self (*ātman*), which is its own nature (*svabhāva*). But surely this [self] is not an object, precisely because it is the inner self; so how can it have the nature of an object?

It is called such because of its attachment to the objects of delusion, just as the intellect (*buddhi*) is so described. Or rather, through the object, the intellect becomes entirely identified with that [object]; thus, the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) are here [the objects], but the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) does not apply to internal or external entities.
It is beyond ratiocination and outside the scope of inference; it is unknowable, meaning it is not within the range of the internal or external senses. || 12.29 ||
And I shall now declare in its entirety the arising of the fruit of these three qualities— whether it be superior, middling, or inferior.

It is promised that the fruit which arises from practicing these three—whether it be superior, inferior, or middling—shall be explained; and it is promised that whatever nature a person possesses when a particular quality is predominant shall be described. (12.30)

Study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, purity, restraint of the senses, performance of righteous deeds, and contemplation of the Self—these are the characteristics of the quality of goodness (sattva). 12.31.

It is proposed that this should be stated as "the definition of the quality characterized by that connection. The term *sāttvika* must somehow be construed [with the whole]. That by which a quality (*guṇa*) is defined is the "definition of the quality" (*guṇalakṣaṇa*). To the question "Of what is that? the connection is: "[Of] the *sāttvika* [state]. The purpose is that even parts belonging to a collective are seen [to be referred to by the name of the whole]. Therefore, this is what is meant: this is the definition of the quality of *sattva*, just as in the expression "Devadatta’s teacher's house. Just as the teacher, though being a subordinate member, is connected with the word "Devadatta," so too should this be understood. The meanings of the words have been explained. (12.31)
Delight in undertaking [tasks], lack of fortitude, embracing what is not a good deed, and constant indulgence in sense objects—these are the characteristics of the quality of passion (rājasa). 12.32.

Delight in the undertaking of actions—whether they be for the sake of desire, for visible results, or for invisible results—and fruitless exertion: this is the characteristic of the *rājasa* (passionate) type. Lack of fortitude is the mind’s lack of composure even when faced with a slight cause of affliction. The mention of "dejection" refers to the abandonment of enthusiasm. An unworthy deed is that which is contrary to worldly custom and sacred scripture; its "acceptance" is the performance thereof. Attachment to sense objects is the constant, repeated engagement with them. (12.32)
Greed, sleepiness, lack of fortitude, cruelty, atheism, deviation from right conduct, mendicancy, and negligence—these are the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas). 12.33.

Greed (*lobha*) is attachment to wealth and other such things. Cruelty (*kraurya*) is the persistence of enmity even over a slight offense. Nihilism (*nāstikya*) is heedlessness (*pramādatā*). A broken way of life (*bhinnavṛttitā*) is the falling away from moral conduct (*śīlabhraṃśa*). By the inclusion of "and" (*ca*), the censure of the learned is implied. Begging (*yāciṣṇutā*) is the state of being a beggar, having that as one's habit. Heedlessness (*pramāda*) is lack of attention; it is disregard for the Dharma and so forth, and for the avoidance of the states of woe (*apāya*). "Sleep" (*svapna*) and "unsteadiness" (*adhṛti*)—here there is an elision of the negative particle *a-* [to form *asvapna* and *adhairya*]. (12.33)
And for these three qualities abiding in the three [states], this should be known as the summary definition of their characteristics in due order. (12.34)

"In the three times"—that is, during the states of equilibrium, increase, and decrease, or during the arising of results that are superior, inferior, and middling—"this" is a reference to what is about to be stated. (12.34)
Whatever action one has done, is doing, or intends to do, and feels shame for—that should be known by the wise as entirely characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas). || 12.35 ||

He demonstrates that temporal reference mentioned in the verse “in the three” (MDh 12.34): “having done,” “doing,” and “about to do. This may occur in all three times, or sometimes in only one of them. “Why did I act thus? How shall I stand before the learned?”—this is shame, and it is mental exhaustion. (12.35)
That action by which one desires abundant fame in this world,
yet does not grieve over its failure to be accomplished— that should be known as rajasic.

The practice of sacrifices, austerities, and religious duties performed with the thought, "May there be praise for me in the world," is for the sake of reputation. For example: giving gifts to crows at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), engaging in debate out of rivalry with a king, or explaining the scriptures to *śūdras*. By the word "abundant" (*puṣkalām*), because it is an adjunct, he states that reputation acts as an auxiliary. If people publicize the dharma of one who is engaged in practicing dharma, such dharma is not a fault. As it has been said: "Just as for the sake of sugarcane... Just as it was stated by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana in the narrative of the *Mahābhārata*:
Just as a farmer intent on sugarcane in the field gathers even grasses and creepers,
so too a man walking upon the path of Dharma attains fame, desires, and wealth.
And when the fruits of actions do not come to fruition, he does not grieve and there is no suffering; or rather, [it means] when actions do not reach completion. 12.36
That which he desires to know in its entirety, that which he does not feel shame in practicing,
and by means of which his own self is satisfied— this is the characteristic mark of the quality of a true being.
This is quite clear. 12.37.
Desire is said to be the characteristic of *tamas*, while purpose is said to be that of *rajas*;
the characteristic of *sattva* is righteousness (*dharma*). Among these, each succeeding one is superior to the preceding.

But surely there is also pleasure (*sukha*) in the realm of desire (*kāma*). In that case, since [the text] states, "That which is conjoined with joy" (MDh 12.27), it follows that this is a characteristic of *sattva*. How then can it be a characteristic of *tamas*? It is replied: here, *tamas* exists as a perception whose form is delusion (*moha*).
Even that is indeed a characteristic of *sattva*, because it has been stated [in MDh 12.26]: "Truth is knowledge."

It is said: here, the state of being an enjoyer and the enjoyed is not intended; rather, it is an excessive longing directed toward sense objects. And in that state, there is no arising of happiness, yet the object remains unmanifest. Because one whose primary motive is desire is devoid of discrimination between what is proper and improper, this state is indeed of the nature of delusion (*moha*). It is this kind of desire that is intended here, and not the eagerness to approach one's own wife during her fertile period as a matter of scriptural duty. (12.38)
But by which quality each of these enters into the cycle of existence,
those I shall explain in brief, for all of this, in their proper order.

Among these qualities, by whichever quality a person enters into which transmigrations—that term *saṃsāra* being synonymous with "state of existence" (gati), meaning the births one attains—this will be explained further on; such is the verse of the formal promise (*pratijñā-śloka*). 12.39.
Those characterized by sattva attain the state of gods, those characterized by rajas the state of humans, and those characterized by tamas the state of animals; this is the eternal threefold destiny.
This general designation of his destiny is based on his qualities. || 12.40 ||
This secondary course of existence is to be understood as threefold and of three kinds—namely, inferior, middling, and superior—according to the distinction between action and knowledge. (12.41)

This threefold secondary [nature], impelled by the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* and the rest, is further divided into three types each—namely, superior, inferior, and middling. Thus, it becomes ninefold. Furthermore, they are infinite due to the distinctions of action and knowledge (*karmavidyā*), owing to the power of wholesome and unwholesome actions, and because of the many varieties of actions arising from intentional and unintentional application. This is what is meant by the phrase "due to the distinctions of action and knowledge" (verse 12.41).
Immovable beings, worms, insects, fish, snakes along with tortoises,
domestic animals, and wild beasts— this is the lowest state of darkness.
Elephants, horses, Śūdras, and despised Mlecchas;
lions, tigers, and boars—these constitute the middling state of darkness (tāmasī gati). || 12.43 ||
Cāraṇas, Suparṇas, and deceitful men,
as well as Rākṣasas and Piśācas— these are the highest destination among those in the quality of darkness (tamas).

Cāraṇas are storytellers, singers, female entertainers, and the like; suparṇas are specific types of birds. "Śūdras" refers to those who are contemptible—this is the connection. Those who hold Brahmins in contempt, those who live off their servants, and those possessed by intoxication, pride, and so forth; as well as the violent, thieves, and others who are similarly censured. (12.42–44)
Jhallas, mallas, and naṭas, as well as men who live by the sword, those addicted to gambling and drinking, and the low-born—this is the rājasic state. 12.45.

*Jhallas* and *mallās* are performers who enter the arena. Among them, the *mallās* are those who fight with their arms; the *jhallās* are those who strike with sticks or live by means of jesting. (12.45)
Kings, Kṣatriyas, and the domestic priests of kings, as well as those whose primary concern is the science of war, constitute the intermediate Rājasa state. (12.46)

Kings are the lords of the realm; the kṣatriyas are their dependents, the local chieftains. Those preeminent in debate discuss one with another the depths of the meaning of the treatises; those preeminent in war are the warriors. (12.46)

The Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and those who are followers of the gods, as well as all the Apsarases—this is the highest destination among those belonging to the quality of passion (rājasī). || 12.47 ||

The Gandharvas and other such beings are gods; their distinction from [the aforementioned] should be understood from the explanatory passages (arthavāda) and the historical narratives (itihāsa). The Vibudhas are gods, and their attendants are the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and so forth. || 12.47 ||
Ascetics, self-restrained practitioners, Brahmins, and the hosts of celestial beings in their vimānas,
as well as the lunar mansions and the Daityas— this is the first, the sāttvika destination.

*Tapasas* are those for whom austerity is primary, such as forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*) and others; *yatayas* are wandering mendicants (*parivrājakas*) and others. By this, he makes it known that the attainment of a birth is not solely due to the species of one's destiny (*gati*), but also from the performance of actions. For *tapasa*s and the like are not certain specific castes; rather, these designations are caused by action. Others, however, think that there are certain regions inhabited on Mount Meru called *yatayaḥ*. It is heard [in scripture]: "Indra gave the *yatayas* to the hyenas" (*PB* 8.1.4).

Vimānas are specific types of celestial vehicles, such as the Puṣpaka and others; those who travel by means of them are the Vaimānikas, certain classes of divine beings who move through the atmosphere. The first [category] is the lowest. 12.48.
Sacrificers, seers, gods, the Vedas, the luminaries, the years, the ancestors, and the Sādhyas— this is the second path, characterized by goodness (sāttvikī gatiḥ).

The Veda is sound distinguished by its sequential order. But surely, in the context of [the classification of] destinies, what relevance is there for insentient things? For sounds and the like are insentient. To say that "sounds and the like are insentient" is to state too little. All these beings, from the gods down to the stationary objects, have bodies as their essence. Among them, all bodies are insentient; it is only their power that is attained in the form of consciousness belonging to the *puruṣa* and so forth. And since the *puruṣa* is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), the bodies presided over by it, though insentient, are said to be sentient.

Therefore, this is what is meant: the Veda is characterized by *sattva*, and through its practice, a *sāttvika* state is attained. It is not, however, that the attainment of the status of being a Veda itself—characterized by *sattva*—is called a *sāttvika* goal. As for the mention of others, it is heard that there are presiding *kṣetrajñas* or Veda-purushas in the world of Varuṇa. 12.49.
Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest—these the wise declare to be the highest state characterized by sattva. || 12.50 ||

The creators of the universe are the Prajāpatis, Marīci and others. Dharma is the meaning of the Veda. Previously, the nature of the Veda was stated; now, its meaning is stated. This implies that the meaning of the nature [of the Veda] is more important. Alternatively, "dharmas" refers to truth and so forth. Their possession of a physical form (vigrahavattva) is to be understood as before. "Mahat" is another name. The unmanifest (avyakta), the primary matter (pradhāna), and primordial nature (prakṛti) have one and the same meaning.

But surely, if the world is a modification (*vikāra*) of *pradhāna*, then since *sattva* predominates in *pradhāna*, it follows that all its modifications must also have a predominance of *sattva*. Consequently, how could there be an excess of *rajas* and *tamas*? Therefore, what was stated [in Manu Smṛti 12.25], "Whichever of these qualities (*guṇa*) is present in the body in its entirety and exceeds [the others]," is untenable.

It is said: this is not intended to mean that the state of being the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is what is to be attained. What then? Three possibilities exist: either the state of non-manifestation (*avyakti*) is to be attained; or it refers to the method of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*); or else this term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) applied to the *pradhāna* is not used in its numerical sense. For this [term] is based on action: because no manifestation (*vyakti*) of it exists, it is "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) due to its lack of clear illumination. And thus its application to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) occurs. Furthermore, its greatness (*mahattva*) is indeed established by virtue of its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*).

But is it not the case that his state is not truly *sāttvika*? For it is so because of the abandonment of the *guṇas*. Indeed, when one becomes free from the notions of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) and "mine" (*mamakāra*), thinking "I am not, nor is anything mine," it is understood that one then attains the state of Brahman. The attainment of Brahman occurs through *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) alone; however, it is those whose nature is predominantly *sattva* who become intent upon knowledge and the like, and not those of *tamas* or *rajas*. It is with this in mind that the "supreme *sāttvika* state" is spoken of.

The other two positions are untenable. For no accomplishment of the purpose of the *puruṣa* occurs by attaining the state of being the primary cause (*pradhāna*), since that is designated as insentient (*acetana*). Indeed, insentience is even more base than stationary objects (*sthāvara*), for some seek out states such as intoxication and fainting which are dependent upon it. Furthermore, the method of direct perception is not possible here because it is not heard [in scripture]; for from the scriptural text, "The Self, indeed, should be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5), it does not follow that "the *pradhāna* should be seen. Therefore, these two terms, "the Great" (*mahat*) and "the Unmanifest" (*avyakta*), refer exclusively to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). 12.50.
Thus has been fully described the entire cycle of worldly existence, consisting of all living beings, which arises from the threefold action and is itself threefold in its threefold nature.

It is threefold by way of its instruments—speech, mind, and body; it is of three kinds according to the distinction of the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth; and it is again threefold according to the distinctions of "superior" and so on. Furthermore, those destinies which are not specifically mentioned here should be understood as included by virtue of their similarity to those already described. This concludes the section on the qualities (*guṇa*). The following verse also serves as an indicator of what is to be said next. (12.51)
Through attachment to the senses and by not practicing the Dharma, the ignorant and lowest of men go to evil states of existence. 12.52.

The discussion of the senses is intended to demonstrate the practice of what is forbidden. Non-practice of the Dharma is the failure to act as instructed by the learned. Since this occurs among the ignorant, he says: "the ignorant. They alone are the lowest of men. And therefore, they go to—that is, they reach—the sinful transmigrations, which are despicable places of birth. Here, the ripening of karma is explained as it is well known. 12.52
Learn now all that specific womb into which this living soul enters in this world, and by what particular karma it does so, in due succession. (12.53)
Having endured terrible hells for many series of years, upon their exhaustion,
those who have committed great sins enter these transmigrations.

Into terrible hells—terrible due to the agony of enduring suffering—into the places of torment belonging to the denizens of hell. At that very moment, there is the exhaustion of karma through the experience of its fruit once the form [of the body] has arisen. Then, when only a slight residue of karma remains, there is the re-entry into saṃsāra.
But why is all karma not experienced right there?

It has been said: hell is the fruit of the activity of the senses, not of one who is tranquil. Furthermore, because activities are opposed to their effects, there is a cessation of activity through its fruit. In this regard, just as for a blazing fire there is burning, emission of flames, consumption, and heat only while it remains active—and not when it is extinguished—so too should it be understood in the case of the hells.

Fire, however, has two states: quiescence and flaming. Hell, by contrast, is always of a single form. Like fires with upward-flaming tongues, karmic actions are subject to increase and decrease. Therefore, when karma has accumulated, there is hell; when it is being depleted, there is experience elsewhere. In that regard, it is logical [to say] "from that, by what remains. (12.53–54)
The slayer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, or a camel; or that of a cow, a goat, a sheep, a deer, or a bird; or even that of a Caṇḍāla or a Pukkasa. (12.55)
A Brahmin who drinks liquor goes to the state of worms, insects, moths, birds that feed on excrement, and indeed of predatory creatures. (12.56)
"Those that eat excrement" refers to crows and the like; "of the predatory" refers to tigers and the like. || 12.56 ||
A Brahmin who is a thief [becomes] thousands of times a spider, a snake, a lizard, aquatic animals, predatory beasts, and Piśācas. (12.57)
The violator of his guru’s bed [is reborn] hundreds of times as grasses, shrubs, and creepers, as well as among carnivorous beasts with fangs, and among those who perform cruel deeds.
Those who perform cruel deeds and are habituated to killing others. || 12.58 ||

Those who eat the flesh of others become carnivorous beasts; those who consume impure things become worms; thieves become creatures that devour one another; and those who consort with women of the lowest castes become pretas. (12.59)

Carnivorous animals are vultures and the like; worms are those that feed on impure matter. They devour one another, just as a large cat devours a cat, or a large fish a small fish, as if they were many different species. Those who consort with women of the lowest castes are the "lowest," such as the Barbaras and others. (12.59)
By entering into union with outcasts, by approaching the wife of another,
and by stealing the property of a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahmarākṣasa.
A man who, out of greed, steals gems, pearls, corals,
and various other jewels, is born among the goldsmiths.
The Hemakartas are birds. || 12.61 ||
By stealing grain one becomes a rat; by stealing bell-metal, a swan; by stealing water, a water-fowl;
by stealing honey, a gadfly; by stealing milk, a crow; by stealing savory food, a dog; and by stealing ghee, a mongoose.
Ākhu means a mouse. || 12.62 ||
The vulture [takes] meat, the cormorant the fat, the oil-drinking bird the oil, the cricket the salt, and the crane the curd. (12.63)
Having stolen silk, one becomes a partridge; having stolen linen, a frog; having stolen cotton cloth, a curlew; having stolen a cow, an iguana; and having stolen molasses, a guḍuha-bird.
Dardura is a young frog. || 12.64 ||
The chuchundarī [eats] auspicious fragrances; the peacock [eats] leaf-vegetables;
the porcupine [eats] various kinds of prepared food; and the śalyaka [eats] unprepared food.
Barhiṇas are peacocks. || 12.65 ||
By stealing fire, one becomes a cricket; by stealing household utensils, a woodpecker;
and by stealing dyed garments, one is born as a jīvajīvaka bird.
A wolf [seizes] a deer; a tiger, a horse; a monkey, fruit and roots; a bear, a woman; a cuckoo, water; a camel, vehicles; and a goat, livestock. (12.67)

Regarding the phrase "water for a swimmer" (MDh 12.62), water intended for drinking is to be understood here. Regarding "the *stokaka* bird [drinking] water," this refers to water for the purpose of sprinkling grain and so forth. And regarding "juice," they say it is the first juice; alternatively, it should be seen as medicinal herbs and the like that have been infused. (MDh 12.62) || 12.67 ||
Having forcibly seized whatever another's property it may be, or having consumed an offering that was not consecrated by sacrifice, a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal. (12.68)
There is nothing here that is, as it were, hidden. || 12.68 ||
Women also, having stolen by this same method, incur the same fault;
they become wives of these very same creatures.
For when the social classes fall away from their respective duties in times of no distress,
they pass through sinful transmigrations and enter into servitude among bandits.

If a Brāhmaṇa, by abandoning his livelihood through such duties as teaching and the like, should subsist on the mode of life of a Kṣatriya or others, then likewise Kṣatriyas and the rest, having fallen from their own duties, experience sinful transmigrations and births among the animal species; when born again in human form, they attain the status of servants among bandits, thieves, and other violent persons. The phrase "in times of non-distress" is a restatement; for since [such actions] are prescribed for times of distress, there is no fault. (12.70)
A Brahmin who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a *preta* named Ulkāmukha, who eats what has been vomited;
and a Kṣatriya becomes a *kūṭapūtana*, who eats impure matter and corpses.

The evil destinies of those who have fallen from their own dharma are demonstrated. He eats what has been vomited. His mouth is burned by a firebrand. *Kuṇapa* means a corpse. *Kūṭapūtana*: his nose becomes foul-smelling; or there is the reading *kaṭapūtana*. A *kaṭapūtana* is a type of *piśāca* or similar being; it is a certain invisible class of spirit that frequents cremation grounds. (12.71)
The Vaiśya Maitrākṣijyotika becomes a preta that feeds on pus;
and the Śūdra, fallen from his own dharma, becomes a Cailāśaka.
*Maitrākṣijyotika* is another term for the speech of a *piśāca*, as explained previously.

Alternatively, it means that light (*jyotis*) exists even in what is called the "friend" (*maitra*). The "member of the friend" (*maitram aṅgam*) is the anus; its "eye-hole" (*akṣivivaram*) is the opening [of the anus].

Others, however, say it refers to an owl. Or, "the friend" (*maitram*) is the light of the sun; the "eye-light" (*akṣa-jyotis*) is sensory vision. For he does not see by means of the light of the sun. (12.72)
To whatever extent those whose nature is directed toward sense objects indulge in them, to that same extent skillfulness in those very things arises for them. 12.73

In order to turn away from the attachment to wife and children and the greed for wealth and so forth—which are seized by the perception of duality—and which possess even a trace of sensual pleasure that acts as an obstacle to the knowledge of the oneness of the Self and stands as its adversary, the nature of worldly existence, namely human birth, is restated exactly as it is, being well-known to all.

To whatever extent they engage with sense objects through habituation—becoming identical with those objects and craving them—they say that for one who has thus engaged, it becomes their very nature by virtue of that [habitual] character. However, for one who partakes [of objects] only occasionally, no longing arises for the recollection of them through such enjoyment and so forth. But he who is utterly base attains identity with them through the cultivation of that [craving], becoming of the same nature as them. This is what is meant by the phrase "to that same degree, proficiency. The term "proficiency" (*kuśalatā*) refers to the state of being of a single flavor (*ekarasībhāva*). Consequently, he is unable to avoid the sense objects.

Such indeed is the course of action: even regarding acts such as approaching one's own wife—which are neither enjoined nor forbidden by the cultured—the [scripture] prohibits them when they are carried out with wealth acquired through improper means or involve specific types of food that are forbidden. (12.73)
Due to the repeated practice of those evil deeds, those of small intelligence encounter sufferings in various wombs here in this world. (12.74)

And thus, due to the repeated practice of those sinful and forbidden actions—let it be as it is said, "Falling occurs through the repeated performance of censurable acts" (cf. MDh 11.181)—they experience sufferings in various births among worms, insects, and the like. 12.74.
There is wandering through the fierce hells such as Tāmisra,
and [suffering] in the Forest of Sword-leaves and other places, as well as being bound and having one's limbs cut off.

The hells previously mentioned, such as *tāmisra* and *andhatāmisra* (MDh 4.88), are [described here]. Among them, *vivartana* is the turning over from one side to another after having remained on one side; or, for those who are unbound or lying supine, it is the binding by trees with leaves sharpened like the edge of a sword. Or, by means of such leaves fixed to the ground—like fragments of plantain leaves—the limbs of the evildoers are cut off. (12.75)
There are various torments, being devoured by crows and owls,
the heat of sand heated like parched grain, and the dreadful Kumbhīpāka hells.
Karambha is mud; for these are cast into jars and cooked by the heat of fire, like grain and other foodstuffs. (12.76)
And he [experienced] births in various wombs that were mostly full of suffering,
as well as constant afflictions from cold and heat, and manifold fears.
"Non-wombs" refers to animals, hungry ghosts, piśācas, and so forth; "birth therein" means taking birth in those realms which abound in suffering. (12.77)
Repeatedly dwelling in the womb, experiencing birth that is truly dreadful,
enduring wooden bonds, and even being sent into the service of others.
The meaning is clear. || 12.78 ||
The separation from kinsmen and loved ones, as well as dwelling with the wicked; the acquisition of wealth and its loss, and the gaining of friends and enemies. || 12.79 ||
And [he saw] old age, which is beyond remedy, and the affliction caused by diseases, and those various kinds of sufferings, and death itself, which is difficult to overcome. (12.80)
These two [verses] also have their meaning already explained. 12.79–80.
With whatever disposition one performs any particular action, with a body of that same nature one experiences its corresponding fruit. (12.81)

Whatever action one performs—whether it be *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, or *tāmasa*—with a disposition that is *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, or *tāmasa*, one reaps a corresponding fruit through such a body, whether it be predominantly *sattva*, *rajas*, or *tamas*: namely, a *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, or *tāmasa* result.

Since this is so, and since from action abounding in *rajas* and *tamas* there arises the attainment of undesirable fruits due to the cause of unwholesome intentions (*akuśala-saṃkalpa*), one must therefore avoid that and act with a deed characterized by wholesome intentions (*kuśala-saṃkalpa*). || 12.81 ||
Thus has the entire arising of the fruits of your actions been declared.
Now learn this action which brings about the supreme good for a Brahmin.

Those actions, both prescribed and prohibited, have been taught as they pertain to the production of their fruits; therefore, one must turn away from them. Since the enjoyment of sensual pleasures is followed by suffering, one should desist from them. One should abide in the ritual injunctions leading to the highest good (*naiḥśreyasa*), which are the means to liberation taught in the section on knowledge (*vidyākāṇḍa*) to be described hereafter. We shall now explain that. (12.82)
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, restraint of the senses, non-violence, and service to the guru are the supreme means for attaining the highest good. 12.83.

By the term *niḥśreyasa* (the supreme good), it is not merely the accomplishment of human goals (*puruṣārtha*) that is expressed, but rather a specific state of joy characterized by the definitive cessation of the association with pleasure and pain. The repetition of the study of the Vedas and other practices mentioned here and there is for the purpose of praising the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*). "Knowledge" refers to that which has the meaning of the Vedas as its object. The other words have meanings already explained. (12.83)
And among all these auspicious actions here, a certain action has been declared to be more conducive to welfare for a person. (12.84)
And for all of these, knowledge of the Self is declared to be supreme;
for that is the foremost of all sciences, since through it immortality is attained. (12.85)

Knowledge of the self (*ātmajñāna*) is twofold: first, the knowledge of the individual soul (*jīva*, *kṣetrajña*, *vijñānātman*), which is a synonym for the self that is distinct from the body, senses, intellect, and so forth; which is established as the agent and enjoyer; which is the object of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*); which is included within the cognition of objects; and which is the enjoyer of the fruits of actions pertaining to future bodies, even though those actions themselves perish upon the destruction of the body. The other is the knowledge of the nature of the eternal, existent, and singular Supreme Self, who is the sole cause of the birth and so forth of the entire universe, who appears in various forms due to the influence of the impressions of ignorance (*avidyāvāsanā*), and who is perceived as one and the same among animals, humans, and others; this is the knowledge of the essential nature as revealed by such scriptural passages as: "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5).

In this context, the thorough knowledge of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) is employed for the performance of ritual actions (*karmavidhi*). For if there were no such entity distinct from the body and so forth to serve as the enjoyer of the fruits of rites performed after death, injunctions such as "one who desires heaven" would be purposeless; consequently, no one would engage in them. Therefore, that [knowledge of the *kṣetrajña*] is useful for the practice of ritual action. However, regarding the knowledge of the oneness of the Supreme Self—which arises through the power of concealing [duality], serving [the teacher], and repeated practice, and which reveals the Self whose nature is pure, awakened, liberated, blissful, eternal, and indestructible—the following is appropriate: "That is the foremost of all sciences, for by it immortality is attained. "Immortality is attained from that" means from the attainment [of that knowledge]. The word "from that" (*tataḥ*) is a designation for the science, namely the science of the Self (*ātmavidyā*). But the knowledge of the *kṣetrajña*, because it is merely an auxiliary to ritual action, does not lead to immortality. Therefore, what is intended by "knowledge of the Self" is the vision of the True Self (*sadātman*), which is the subject of both duality and non-duality as taught in the Vedānta. (12.85)
Of these six aforementioned types of actions, it should be known that the Vedic rite is always more conducive to welfare, both in this world and after death.

The six duties, beginning with the study of the Vedas, are conducive to spiritual welfare (*śreyas*). Among these, Vedic rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma possess the quality of bringing about the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). It is within these that liberation (*mokṣa*) is realized.

But surely, if the genitive in *pūrveṣām* (of the former) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), that is untenable. For selection occurs when a specific member of a collective group is distinguished by some attribute that applies to that same domain, yet is not possible for other members within that group—such as in the expression, “Among humans, the Kṣatriya is the most heroic,” where the Kṣatriya, being included within the class of humans, is singled out by his supreme heroism. How can there be a selection of what has not been mentioned and what is not included? And here, Vedic ritual action and the like have not been previously mentioned.

Now it is said: [Objection: Since the study of the Vedas (*antarvedābhyāsa*) and so forth are themselves Vedic, how can Vedic action be considered "unspecified"? [Response: If that were the case, then because the general is [already included] within the general, there would be even less determination [of what is specifically meant]. For it is not the case that one says, "Among cows, the cow that has just given milk is the best. For if non-Vedic actions were indeed those whose purpose was specified, then one might look to them and conclude that the Vedic is more conducive to the highest good (*śreyaskaratara*).

Furthermore, what exactly are the Vedic rites intended here? If they refer to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such sacrifices, then an authority for this specific selection must be stated, since the study of the Vedas and similar acts are also Vedic. If it is argued that "those are not Vedic because they are Smārta (based on Smṛti), and only those enjoined by direct Śruti are Vedic," this is not so; for the study of the Vedas and the like are not included as constituent parts within all Vedic rites. This is precisely what [the author] will state later: "They are included, respectively, in that injunction of action" (MDh 12.87). If that were not the case, then in the Agnihotra and other rites, great austerity would have to be performed. There is no purpose served by that statement of his. Both the study of the Vedas and the like are to be practiced, as are the Agnihotra and the like. In that regard, we do not know what kind of superior merit these possess. Nor are their fruits equal, such that one could speak thus based solely on the excellence of the fruit. For example, from the gift of a cow comes heaven, and from the Jyotiṣṭoma comes its persistence over a long period of time. As it has been said: "As in the world, there may be a distinction in the fruit according to the magnitude [of the cause]" (PMS 1.2.17).

To this it is replied: regarding the statement that no purpose is served by what was said [in verse 141], some say as follows: the declaration that Vedic [texts] are more conducive to the highest good (*śreyaskarataratva*) is for the purpose of making known their subverting power (*bādhakatva*) over Smṛti when there is a contradiction. As it has been stated: "When there is a contradiction between two [injunctions] of equal strength, there is an option (*vikalpa*)" (GDh 1.4); thus, a Smṛti of unequal strength is sublated by Śruti. Furthermore: "But where there may be a conflict between two Śrutis, both are remembered as Dharma" (MDh 2.14). When there is a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, it follows by implication that the Smṛti is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Since this has already been understood from what precedes, it need not be stated;

however, there is no fault in stating it again for the sake of clarification. Alternatively, another meaning is also possible: [the mention of] "pure" refers to the statement regarding options (*vikalpa*). In cases of conflict between two Smṛti texts, it is not for the purpose of providing an option. Therefore, the meaning is this: Vedic injunctions are more authoritative than those based on Smṛti. The mention of "Vedic study and so forth" is intended to illustrate all Smṛti-based matters. It is recited in this way merely for the sake of metrical conformity.

We, however, say: this matter is established by logic (*nyāya*); yet, even for that which is established by logic, it is appropriate to state it out of friendship. Here, the knowledge of the Self (*ātman*) is recited at every step. In that case, what occasion is there for its sublation? Furthermore, the authors of the *Smṛtis* ought not to seek to validate their own statements by means of their own statements alone. Now, if it is argued: "The injunction stated belongs to the *Yājñavalkīya-smṛti*, not to our own; it is merely a similarity," then that which is said regarding our own [text] is as follows: therefore, in accordance with the context, the term "study of the Vedas" (*vedābhyāsa*) and so forth is distinct [from the knowledge of the Self]. This is not recited here after having first made a formal proposition regarding the Self. And how is it that they have explained the knowledge of the Self as being subordinate to the Śruti? [From the study of the Vedas and so forth,] Vedic ritual action such as sacrifice is superior; from that comes the knowledge of the inner self (*adhyātma-jñāna*). Otherwise, what is stated in one place would be lost in another and fall elsewhere, as if it were something other than the progeny [of the same subject].

Alternatively, the knowledge of the self (*ātmajñāna*) alone is what is Vedic here, because the Veda is intent upon its exposition. The instruction on the *agnihotra* and other rites is for the purpose of engaging children and others, like the instruction on taking medicine for the sake of growth.

Alternatively, the proponents of Brahman (brahmavādinaḥ) understand that the entire status of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) as enjoined by the Śruti and other scriptures serves as an aid to qualification (*adhikāra*). This is because the disciplined ones, having shaken off this innate ignorance—which is the cause of attachment to the objects of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—through the power of the impressions from the study of the scriptures, gradually develop detachment. Consequently, their firm grip of thirst and passion becomes loosened, and they become fit to be directed toward the instruction concerning the highest qualification. Therefore, this statement—"Vedic action is to be known as more conducive to the highest good in every way"—refers to the type of action called "renunciation" (*nivṛtti*) which will be discussed hereafter.

Alternatively, if there were a distinction [between the two views], then even for all those who hold the view that both [the waking and dreaming states] are unreal like a dream, the knowledge of the oneness of the Self would be the highest good (*śreyas*). Therefore, the study of the Vedas and so forth, which are prompted by the teaching of duality, must be performed. However, the objection regarding the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) has already been resolved by those very [arguments], because distinctness is established through something else superimposed by the intellect, as in the example: "The people of Mathurā are wealthier than those of Pāṭalīputra. If it is argued that in such a case this would be a fifth [case-ending, the ablative], here too a rebuttal has been provided, since there is no difference in the underlying property (*dharma*). (12.86)
But in the Vedic path of action, all these [stages] without exception are included, respectively, within each specific ritual injunction.

They describe Vedic action as consisting of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites. The application of the verse to these very [actions] is as follows: *kriyāvidhiḥ* (the injunction of action) refers to the Vedic *karmavidhiḥ* (injunction of ritual action). In the context of *karmayoga*—that is, the performance of ritual action—the external states to be accomplished are included within these practices, such as the study of the Upaniṣads and the Vedas.
