By the word *tasmin* ("in that"), he indicates that some of these are equally included within it by virtue of being pervaded (*vyāpyatayā*). When "karmayoga" is mentioned, the inclusion of the term "kriyāvidhi" is for the purpose of completing the meter; or alternatively, the distinction may be explained according to the classification of Soma sacrifices, as in the rule *kratuyajñebhyaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.68).

In that regard, the study of the Vedas (*vedābhyāsa*) is included within the sacrificial session (*satra*), because it is utilized everywhere in the mantras of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Austerity (*tapas*) is present in the initiations (*dīkṣā*), the attendant rites (*upasad*), and the Soma sacrifices, as indicated by such texts as, "Milk is the nectar of the Brāhmaṇa. Knowledge (*jñāna*) is present everywhere, since those who possess [worldly] knowledge lack the qualification [for the sacrifice]. Likewise, the restraint of the senses (*indriyasaṃyama*) pertains to each specific rite, as in: "One should not approach a woman; one should not eat meat. Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is also present, as in: "On this night, one should not sever the life-breath of any living being, even that of a lizard" (BĀU 1.5.14). Thus, there is no application of [the rules for] service to the teacher and so forth.
However, for those who maintain that karma has indeed ceased, this verse serves the purpose of ensuring the continued practice of Vedic study and other such duties.

Even for one devoted to meditation (*upāsana*), these duties are included because they are performed; thus, the injunctions for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) found in the Upaniṣads for the meditator are intended for the destruction of sin, and do not imply that there is any modification of the prescribed remedies. Therefore, when there is the non-performance of what is enjoined or the performance of what is prohibited, demerit (*pratyavāya*) arises.
If this is so, then from where would liberation come?

Through the experience of the fruits [of past actions], there is the destruction of the evil accumulated in other births; through non-performance, [there is the destruction] of that which was previously intended by one's own intellect; through the excellence of practice in breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and specific forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), there is the performance of expiation for what was done through negligence; and through the direct realization of the nature of the Self as free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*). One should first cause that [Self] to be known; liberation (*mokṣa*) is the attainment of its state. For this reason, even one intent on being established in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭha*) must perform the study of the Vedas and other such duties. Regarding each person for whom the renunciation of action (*karmasaṃnyāsa*) is prescribed in scripture, that has been explained in the sixth [chapter].

The procedure for ritual action (*kriyāvidhi*) is indeed the procedure for worship (*upāsanavidhi*), as enjoined by such passages as, “He is to be seen, He is to be heard” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5). And because there are many modes of worship, the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*)—expressed as “in this and in that”—is entirely appropriate. Therefore, in some instances, such as “One should worship Him as Brahman” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.1), “This golden person who is in the sun” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.6), and “And this Self is free from evil” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1), the injunction is directed toward [the Lord] as superimposed upon the intellect and other faculties already grasped; in others, such as the passage concerning the golden one, it is the worship of that very same [Lord] through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and in yet others, by virtue of His sovereignty over all worship, there is the injunction regarding the stainless Self, such as “He is below, He is above” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.1). Thus, due to the multiplicity of these injunctions, the distributive repetition is justified. (12.87)
Vedic action is of two kinds: that which leads to worldly prosperity and that which leads to the supreme good; it is also twofold, being either active engagement or withdrawal.
But has it not already been explained that Vedic action is exclusively *pravṛtta* (active)? Why is it now said to be of two kinds?
This is not a fault. It was the predominance of the *pravṛtta* Vedic [action] that was explained there; however, the Vedic [nature] is uniform throughout.

One attains and is reborn in happiness. Furthermore, the term *sukhābhyudayika* should be understood etymologically (*anvartha*) as "that which has happiness and worldly prosperity as its purpose," or according to some, "that which has the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) as its purpose. In the context of the words "active" (*pravṛtta*) and "withdrawn" (*nivṛtta*), these should be connected respectively as previously explained. 12.88.
Action performed with desire for results here or hereafter is called "pravṛtta" (active); but action free from desire and preceded by knowledge is taught as "nivṛtta" (withdrawn).

In this world, there are rites such as the *Kārīrī* and the *Vaiśvānarī*; in the next world, there are rites such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* that accomplish desired ends (*kāmya*). That which is desired is called "desirable" (*kāmya*). Because the fruit is desirable, the action that is its means is also called "desirable. That which is performed without desire is "constant" (*nitya*). Knowledge is the prerequisite for both; for one who lacks knowledge has no entitlement [to perform these rites]. Nevertheless, knowledge is taught for those entitled to the secret [Upaniṣads]. In that case, it is not a prerequisite for both. Furthermore, the word "prior" (*pūrva*) indicates the sense of "first" (*ādi*). The analysis of the compound is: "that of which knowledge is the first, that is, the primary. He who is foremost obtains the ritual first. Therefore, this is what is meant: knowledge is the principal thing and should be practiced primarily; however, the study of the Vedas and so forth is merely according to the requirements of the scriptures. (12.89)
By practicing active (pravṛtta) karma, one attains equality with the gods;
but by practicing renunciation (nivṛtta), one indeed transcends the five elements.

But has it not been stated that desire-driven (*kāmya*) action is characterized by active engagement? Furthermore, some desire-driven acts have heaven as their fruit, while others have perceptible fruits; yet no perceptible action has heaven-like equality (*devasāmyatā*) as its fruit. Therefore, why is it said that one "attains equality with the gods"? Even those rites such as the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, whose specific fruits are not mentioned in scripture, have heaven as their fruit when performed without desire. Consequently, we do not understand how the attainment of equality with the gods could be the fruit of ritual action. Nor can it be argued: "Those actions whose fruits are heard in scripture should be performed without desire, and when so performed, they result in the fruit of divinity. For such an argument would involve the abandonment of what is explicitly stated in scripture and the postulation of what is not. Moreover, the fruit in the Veda is something desired, as in "one desiring a village" or "one desiring heaven"; it does not arise from the inherent nature of things, like the consumption of poison. If you say that the attainment of divinity and so forth occurs even though it is not desired, that is a contradiction. If it is asked how there can be a lack of desire in the context of prohibitions (*pratiṣedhādhikāra*), the answer is that in those cases, the very state [of non-transgression] is connected as the fruit. Indeed, what is undesirable cannot be desired. Now, if the fruit of the obligatory (*nitya*) rites is stated here [as attaining divinity], then their status as obligatory is lost. Furthermore, by terms such as "as long as one lives," the fact that they have an obligatory fruit is understood. If a fruit must necessarily be postulated, let the avoidance of transgression (*pratyavāya*) be postulated. For that, being postulated, is not inconsistent with their obligatory nature.

Regarding the subsequent verse, "He indeed transcends the five elements," we do not understand it here in the sense that he "transcends" them means he is "liberated. Elsewhere, *atyaya* is said to mean dissolution (*laya*). However, the dissolution of the individual soul (*jīva*) within the elements is not intended here; rather, what is meant is the attainment of the nature of Brahman.

Others also explain it thus: "And he transcends the five elements; his body does not consist of the five elements, but rather follows as a mere form of light (*tejomūrti*). But even that is nothing; for liberation is indeed the non-grasping of a body. Whether that body consists of one element or of the five elements, what difference does it make regarding its state of transmigrating? Therefore, this verse must be explained [otherwise]."

It is said in reply: As for what was stated—"To which action does the fruit of equality with the gods belong? Because obligatory (*nitya*) rites have no fruit, and because optional (*kāmya*) rites are connected with other fruits"—to that we say: By this, it is not meant that this fruit belongs to all Vedic actions. What then? It refers to the fruit of the *nivṛtta* (renounced) action, wherein there is engagement. Furthermore, it is a praise [of the path], implying: "What action exists by which that fruit is attained? And indeed, there are certain actions whose fruit is the attainment of godhood. Therefore, this is what is being said: That which is known in the *Karmakāṇḍa* as something to be performed—its highest goal is the attainment of godhood, but not liberation (*mokṣa*). However, the action taught in the section on the secret doctrine (*rahasyādhikāra*) is the cause of non-return. In that regard, for one who desires, the action is a cause of bondage because it is impaired by the mental resolve for a fruit. For such is the nature of actions that they initiate the body and its instruments for the sake of yielding their own fruit. Likewise, even the obligatory rites, if not performed, become causes of transgression (*pratyavāya*); those too certainly initiate a body.

If this were so, he would perform the obligatory (*nitya*) rites, and he would not perform the optional (*kāmya*) or prohibited (*pratiṣiddha*) ones; because of the absence of karma that initiates a body, he would attain liberation due to the absence of its cause. What, then, would be the use of the knowledge of the Self? As it has been said: "One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites with the desire to avoid transgression; one who is devoid of [the desire for] liberation should engage in those [rites], as well as in the optional and prohibited ones. (Ślokavārttika 5.15: 110)

Thus it has been stated by the Blessed Ones: for one who does not practice knowledge (*vidyā*), there is no destruction of ignorance (*avidyā*); and as long as ignorance is not severed by knowledge, there is no attainment of the nature of Brahman. With this very intent, it was said: "Free from desire and preceded by knowledge" (MDh 12.89), and likewise, "To have desire as one's essence is not praised" (MDh 2.2). *Sāmyatā* is the state of being equal in action; its meaning is that one attains a state equal to that of the gods.

Furthermore, the delusion regarding this [Self] that it "transcends all beings" is also not tenable. Even "deceit" (*vipralāpana*) is said to be "transcending" (*atyaya*); the meaning is that one becomes the entire manifold of frost-like phenomena.
Even with the reading "he approaches" (*abhyeti*), the state of being bodiless (*aśarīratva*) is expressed. 12.90.

Furthermore, as to how this elaboration (prapañca) is to be performed, he says: "Seeing the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, equally, the one who sacrifices to the Self attains self-sovereignty. (12.91)

By the word *bhūta*, everything that exists—whether moving or stationary, sentient or insentient—is denoted. Within that, one should perceive the Self, thinking: "This world is just like me. And so says the Śruti: "I am the swaying branch of the tree" (TU 1.10.1). One should abandon the conventional distinction between self and other. Bondage arises from the notions: "This is I," "this is mine," and "this is not mine. For one who has abandoned the obsession with "self" and "mine" and has relinquished the distinction between self and other, the absolute oneness of the Self alone shines forth. This indeed is the meaning of the state of *svārājya* (sovereignty).

"All beings in myself. That very world, which consists of the manifold expansion of transformations, exists within me; thus it is realized that I alone am the creator, the agent, the meditator, and the object of meditation. One who sacrifices to the Self (*ātmayājī*): he who worships and regards the Self alone as comprising all deities, seeing thus—"Neither fire nor the sun is the deity; I alone am the deity"—becomes one who sacrifices to the Self. However, it is not enjoined that a sacrifice must be performed with the Self as its objective.
Some say: in the [offerings] to Agni and others, the deities such as Agni should not be spoken of even as one's own self (ātman).

Sovereignty (*svārājya*): existing in one's own kingdom is *svārājya*. One becomes independent like the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and becomes self-luminous. One does not depend on the light of the moon, the sun, and so forth, nor on the senses such as the eyes, nor on the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) such as the mind. Therefore, it is said "seeing" (*paśyan*); it is stated that one should cultivate this (*bhāvayet*). It is not mere seeing; rather, when all external and internal activities have been set aside, those intent upon that cultivation are remembered [as liberated]. (12.91)
Even having abandoned the aforementioned ritual acts, the best of the twice-born should be diligent in self-knowledge, tranquility, and the study of the Vedas.

Regarding the phrase "even the aforementioned actions": this does not prescribe the abandonment of rituals such as the *agnihotra*; rather, it prescribes the practice of the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), meaning that one should exert effort toward the realization of the Self. The basis for the instruction to "abandon actions" is that one should practice the knowledge of the Self even while performing acts such as circumambulating sacred sites of exalted deities, reciting mantras, and approaching teachers. For there is no voluntary renunciation of obligatory duties (*nitya-karma*); [such renunciation] is not prescribed among the duties of a person (*puruṣadharma*) and so forth. (12.92)
For this indeed is the fulfillment of the purpose of birth, especially for a Brahmin;
having attained this, the twice-born becomes one who has accomplished his duty, and not otherwise.

The term *dvija* (twice-born) indicates that even Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas have the qualification for the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*). This is shown by the *Āraṇyaka* scripture: "Especially for the Brāhmaṇa. [The phrase from verse 12.92], "in the study of the Vedas," should be connected here. For it is only through the practice of equanimity by one who knows the Self that these two [the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya] are possible. Having attained the knowledge of the Self, the twice-born becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done; by this much, the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*) is completed. Indeed, there is no goal of human life other than liberation (*mokṣa*). 12.93.

Now, it may be argued that what was stated—that one should perceive this [reality] through the oneness of the self of all—is as if contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For by direct perception, an entity appears as distinct. Therefore, how can it be grasped as one? This would be teaching something for its own sake without beginning [in a practical context]. How is it possible to see the distinct as non-distinct? Indeed, a donkey cannot be grasped by the intellect as a cow. In the case of mother-of-pearl and the like, it is perceived as having the form of silver due to a defect in the sense organ, appearing in a manner other than it truly is; it is not so from instruction. For one who instructs [on the nature of an object], one recognizes that elephant; such a person would not directly obtain the fruit of the word. To this, he says:
The Veda is the eternal eye for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings;
it is impossible to master and immeasurable—such is the established nature of the Vedic scripture.

This is the meaning: here, the Veda is the authority (*pramāṇa*) for the speaker. It is like an eye, by virtue of the commonality of being a cause of vision. Just as a cognition of form arises without effort regarding objects delimited by the eye, so too [it arises] from the Veda; thus it is called "the eye. It is "sanātana," meaning eternal, constant, and perpetual. By this, he states its non-human origin. For if it were of human origin, there would be no authority for its validity, since even error is possible; therefore, because there is no certainty regarding the presence or absence of qualities or defects in a person, the Veda is authoritative by virtue of its being non-human (*apauruṣeya*). Consequently, due to the authority of the Veda, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the object that is perceived.
But surely, if one were to teach in this way—"one should sprinkle with fire and kindle with water"—would there not be a contradiction?

This is an unequal comparison. For in that case [of perception], an object that is already perceived through the power of the thing itself is taught as something to be performed; thus, that object falls within the scope of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Because it is the opposite of that, what has been stated is appropriate. But here, since the words are subordinate to an injunction (*vidhi*), and other means of knowledge do not have an injunction as their object—having instead as their scope established entities whose nature is already accomplished—how can there be a contradiction when there is no single common object?

For here, indeed, the vision of things that are non-self as being the self is enjoined for the sake of the fruit of sovereign power (*svārājya*). In this regard, where there is an excessive perception of difference, it is possible to alter that through practice. For instance, mental states such as passion and the like can be restrained by the practice of the limbs of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) through their excellence; likewise, even toward an object of hatred, the notion of "being hated" ceases through loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth—this is both seen and personally experienced by everyone. By the power of cultivation, the nature of a non-existent thing appears; just as in a case of deception, lovers see everything as if it were their beloved—how much more so when there is actual oneness? How then could it appear as differentiated, given that it is contradictory to its true form? Indeed, all cultivation takes that [oneness] as its form, yet it exists as differentiated. And in this context, such a vision is enjoined as equality, wherein the notions "this is mine" and "this is not mine" are untenable. As it has been said:

"‘It is mine’—these two syllables are death; ‘it is not mine’—this is the eternal. (MBh 14.13.3). Therefore, there is no contradiction. The Vedic passages beginning with "of the ancestors, gods, and humans" [264] imply that even the gods and others possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) when endowed with such [knowledge], yet they do not perceive objects beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) in this manner, because it is impossible to know them without the Śruti. Furthermore, it is "immeasurable" (*aprameya*) and "unlimited" (*aparimāṇa*) because the branches of the Veda (*veda-śākhā*) are infinite. Moreover, it is "incapable of being measured" in terms of its actual meaning. The term *veda-śāstra* refers to the Vedas. 12.94.
Whatever scriptures are outside the Veda, and whatever false views there may be—
all of them are fruitless after death, for they are remembered as being grounded in darkness.

Previously, the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the Veda was stated on the basis of its being non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*); now, the lack of authority of those Vedas that are of human origin is addressed. Furthermore, there are scriptural injunctions (*codanā*) outside the Veda, contrary to the Veda, and not rooted in the Veda, compiled into treatises—such as the well-known doctrines of the Nirgranthas (Jains) and others, like "Heaven is attained by worshipping a *caitya*. These are "false views" (*kudṛṣṭi*), which are systems of unsound reasoning. False views include the proof of a creator of the Veda, the refutation of the *apūrva*, the deities, and so forth. All of these are fruitless after death—that is, when their ultimate consequence is reached. They are said to be ultimately fruitless because they are established through reasons and examples that are, in fact, fallacious; for those arguments are merely semblances of logic (*yuktīnām ābhāsa*). And those arguments, though appearing in the form of concise summaries, expand into vast treatises that lead one astray onto another path. Likewise, there is no authority in the teachings of those of human origin, because humans lack the capacity to perceive supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*); and even if such capacity existed, there would be no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the teacher [to prove his claim]. No proof applies here to the effect that "this person is omniscient, and therefore this scripture was composed by him. Even if authorship were admitted, it would entail the necessity of postulating unseen things based on seen ones; and if that were accepted as authoritative, it would result in the establishment of [the author's] divinity. Thus, the meaning is that those arguments are rooted in delusion.

Others, however, explain: "After death" (*pretya*) means that those [actions] are fruitless for one who has died, because they result in a state of darkness (*tamas*), being the cause of birth in a *tāmasa* womb.

On this view, since there is no common agent [for the action of dying and the attainment of results], the form *pretya* is difficult to justify; alternatively, a locative case derived from a word ending in *-niṣṭha* should be read as "in death" (*prete*). (12.95)
Whatever other things there may be besides these, which arise and perish, are fruitless and false because they belong to a limited, temporal duration. (12.96)

Therefore, those other teachings that arise from the Veda are subject to arising and perishing; because they are characterized by arising and perishing, they are impermanent. The Veda, however, is eternal because it is the opposite of that. Since they are of recent origin—having been composed by some person of the present day—they are fruitless, as there is no invisible result (*adṛṣṭa*) [to be attained]. Whatever [teachings] exist, such as those characterized by being rooted in deception and so forth, [are likewise fruitless]. (12.96)
The four castes, the three worlds, and the four stages of life in their distinctness—the past, the present, and the future—all are established through the Veda. (12.97)

This too is indeed a praise [of the Veda]. The fourfold caste system (*cāturvarṇya*) is established through the Veda; it exists as the basis for qualification, as in such passages as: "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa; in summer, a Rājanya" (ĀpDh 1.1.19), and so forth. Its essential nature (*svarūpa*), however, is to be understood through worldly usage, since it is common to all castes, as has been shown elsewhere. The three worlds—"From here, the gods subsist upon offerings"—by this, the fact that the Veda is the cause of the existence of the triple world is already established, as the Smṛtis are rooted in the Veda. The stages of life (*āśrama*) also arise from the Veda alone. Regarding the past (*bhūta*)—the joys and sorrows of previous births—and that which is present (*bhavat*) or that which will be (*bhaviṣyat*), the Veda alone is the refuge for all of it. (12.97)
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these are established from the Veda alone; their origin arises from qualities and actions.

The establishment of sound and other objects as means of pleasure, by virtue of their being things to be enjoyed, occurs through the Veda alone. From the performance of Vedic rituals, there arises the occurrence of sounds such as songs; from the abandonment of those [rituals], there is the hearing of harsh sounds. Therefore, the intended meaning is this: sound and the other qualities that initiate the body present themselves to the two [the organs of hearing and speech] as their respective objects, and thus they are established through the Veda. However, the Veda is not the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) [of the body]. Hence, "sound and the others which initiate the body [are established] for those two. He states exactly this: "Production [results] from the action of the qualities (*guṇa*). Production is the arising of sound and the others. For that purpose, there is the action of the qualities. And because it is for the sake of a result, the primary action (*pradhāna-karma*), such as the *Citrā* sacrifice, is said to be the property of the qualities (*guṇa-dharma*).

An alternative reading is: “*prasūtir guṇadharmataḥ*. The *guṇas* are *sattva* and the others; their *dharma* is transformation (*vipariṇāma*). The production (*prasūti*) of that [transformation] consists in its departure from the state of equilibrium, its intensification, and its diversification. In this regard, the Veda alone is the cause, because it has the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) as its motive. Other variant readings concerning diversity are not recorded here, as they serve no purpose. (12.98)
The eternal Vedic scripture sustains all beings;
therefore, I consider this to be the supreme means for the accomplishment of a living being.

[299] Furthermore, the support of all beings is demonstrated in the Vedic scripture (*veda-śāstra*) for the *brāhmaṇa*. Thus it is said: "The oblation (*havis*) is offered into the fire; that fire causes the sun to rise; the sun, by means of its rays, causes rain to fall; from that, nourishment (*ārtti*) arises; from that, indeed, their birth and subsistence are known as the oblation. Here too it is stated: "An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun," and so forth (MDh 3.66). [300] [301] From that, indeed, their birth and subsistence are known as the oblation. Here too it is stated: "An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun," and so forth (MDh 3.66).

Therefore, I consider this to be the supreme cause for the fulfillment of human goals: namely, that the instruction on Dharma for this living being is given by such means, and from this cause, the logical justification for those [teachings] is as it has been shown. Now, if the purpose is based on material acquisition (*aupādānika*), why is it called "worldly purpose" (*laukika*)? It is said in reply: its performance is Vedic, but because its result is visible, it is indeed worldly. (12.99)
One who is learned in the Vedic scriptures deserves the command of an army, the sovereignty of a kingdom, the office of a judge, and even the lordship over all the worlds. (12.100)

This is an excessive praise. "Punishers" (*daṇḍanetāraḥ*) refers to the leaders of punishment, those appointed to oversee what has been done and what remains undone in villages and cities. An "army" (*senā*) consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; its "lord" is the commander. "Kingdom" (*rājyam*) is the status of a regional ruler (*maṇḍaleśvaratva*). "Sovereignty over all the world" (*sarvalokādhipatyam*) is the status of a universal monarch (*sārvabhaumatva*). || 12.100 ||
Just as a fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees, so does one who knows the Vedas burn away the faults of his own past actions. 12.101
This also is as before; the construction of the words is clear and the meanings of the terms are well-known. (12.101)
One who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, dwelling in whatever stage of life he may be,
becomes fit for union with Brahman even while remaining in this very world.

"For the state of Brahman" (*brahmabhūyāya*) means for the condition of being Brahman (*brahmabhāvāya*), that is to say, for the attainment of the nature of Brahman. "Where" (*yatra*) refers to even after emerging from that [state], or by way of reversal. As it has been said: "And having emerged even from hostility, the Brahmins, having announced their intent, go forth on the mendicant's round. (12.102)

Those who possess the texts are superior to the ignorant; those who retain them are better than those who merely possess them; those who have knowledge are superior to those who merely retain them; and those who apply themselves with resolve are superior to those who merely possess knowledge. (12.103)

The ignorant (*ajña*) are fools who have not studied. The "bookish" (*granthin*) are the learned who merely recite the texts. Among them, the "retainers" (*dhārin*) are those who study with great effort, whereas the former study without much diligence. The word "of the text" (*granthasya*) is connected there as well, meaning "retainers of the text. Their superiority arises from their eligibility for activities such as *japa* (recitation) and receiving gifts; however, the possessors of knowledge (*jñānin*) are superior still, as they are eligible for everything. When *japa* and other rites are performed preceded by knowledge, they yield an excellence of fruit. As it has been said: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), that alone becomes more powerful" (ChU 1.1.10). The "resolute" (*vyavasāyin*) are practitioners free from doubt, for whom it is impossible to think otherwise than this.
This also is for the purpose of praise: the Vedas are capable of leading to the goals of human life through mere study alone; how much more so, then, the knowledge of their meaning! 12.103.
Austerity and knowledge are the supreme means for a Brahmin to attain the highest good;
by austerity one destroys sin, and through knowledge one partakes of immortality.

By this he shows the following: even when knowledge exists, there is no liberation for one whose sins are not exhausted; and even when the exhaustion of karma exists, there is no liberation if the knowledge of the Self does not exist. Therefore, what was stated—that "they are liberated by their very nature"—is incorrect. Immortality is non-return [to saṃsāra], which is this state consisting of absolute bliss. 12.104
Perception, inference, and scripture consisting of various traditions—these three must be well understood by one who desires the purification of dharma. 12.105

Having become a friend, he teaches worldly matters. *Dharma* is the meaning of the Vedas; its "purification" (*śuddhi*) is its exposition, which consists in establishing the definitive conclusion (*siddhānta*) by refuting opposing views (*pūrvapakṣa*). This occurs when there is certainty regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest. For when perception is well-understood, one recognizes [the flame] despite the difference in the flame's various stages through the process of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Thus, the permanence of sound and so forth is established. However, for one who lacks correct discrimination (*viveka*), perception would result in an indistinct determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding both [the flame and the sound]. Having observed the decay of the flame and other such things through perception, one might likewise suspect it in the case of sound; consequently, the Veda would consist of a collection of non-eternal sounds. But for one who has cultivated expertise in the valid means of knowledge, who does not entertain the notion that the apprehension of sound is based on a failure to grasp its true nature—just as one who knows the flame [does not mistake] the basis for perceiving its difference [from moment to moment]—such a person does not imagine that the sublation (*bādha*) seen in the flame applies to sound, even though there is a distinction between the two, such as whiteness and variegation.

In this way, inference (*anumāna*) too, when well-analyzed, does not serve merely as an indicator for the authority of texts such as the *Mahābhārata*. Through it, one achieves proficiency at the conclusion of treatises on valor and the like. For he who has not analyzed inference, thinking that the operation of inference occurs merely through the observation and non-observation of the subject (*pakṣa*) and the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), might even postulate an author for the Veda. But when one becomes a person of subtle intellect, one determines its lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) because there is no evidence of an agent—characterized by the necessity of bathing after study—who could be its creator.

And the scripture (*śāstra*) consists of various traditions (*āgama*). Because it contains various injunctions and prohibitions, its tradition is manifold and of many kinds. That wherein one arrives [at knowledge] is a tradition. Due to the many branches of the Veda and the distinction between *śruti* and *smṛti*, its diversity has been stated. And this matter is implied by the injunction for self-study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) and is taught out of friendship; yet neither of these two is merely for the sake of praise. (12.105)
He who investigates the instruction on dharma given by the seers with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedas and the Shastras—he, and no other, knows dharma. 12.106.

The *ṛṣi* is the Veda; that which originates therein is *ārṣa*. This refers to the instruction on Dharma that is Vedic. The syntactical construction of the words is: he who investigates by means of reasoning—that is, by other forms of inference and logic—knows Dharma.

*Tarka* (reasoning) is the internal accomplishment of *ūha* (adaptation) and *apoha* (exclusion), such that one determines: "this is appropriate to be adapted here," and "this is to be excluded. For example, in the ritual for the Sun (*saurya*), when the mantra for the pouring out of the oblation—originally obtained from the archetype—as "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour thee out, acceptable to Agni" (VS 2.11)—is in use, the word *agni* is excluded because its referent is not applicable, and the word *sūrya* is inserted. This reasoning does not contradict the Veda. However, he who thinks: "Since there is no deity Agni in the ritual for the Sun, and since mantras are to be employed according to their meaning, and since a mantra ceases to be a mantra if even a single part is altered, the entire mantra must be omitted"—this is a reasoning that contradicts the meaning of the Veda. Furthermore, he who maintains that the employment of mantras consists merely in their recitation, thinking "therefore the mantra should be used exactly as it is, without modification," his reasoning also contradicts the sacred scripture (*śāstra*).

And this is not an injunction; it is an explanatory statement (arthavāda). Its purport here is that such indifference [toward Mīmāṃsā] is known from this very investigation; therefore, by this, the necessity of studying Mīmāṃsā for the sake of the purification of Dharma is enjoined.

Others, however, explain it as follows: by the phrase "by means of reasoning" (*tarkena*), those treatises that prioritize reasoning—namely, the Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, and Lokāyata systems which are devoted to defining worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—are indicated. Among these, the systems of the Buddhists, Lokāyatas, Nirgranthas, and others, which contradict the Veda, are excluded. These [latter] contradict the Veda; the Veda is not a means of valid cognition for them. For in the systems of Kapila, Kaṇāda, Kriyā, Aviratha, Tāntrika, Nigraha-anta, and so forth, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is the means of valid cognition. Accordingly, the Sūtra of Akṣapāda states: "Perception, inference, analogy, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.3). The Vaiśeṣikas also say: "The authority of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) is due to its being His word" (Vaiśeṣikasūtra 1.1.3). Therefore, it follows that those scriptures should be heard. And thus it was shown by the Blessed Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana in the Mahābhārata:

"O King, these dull-witted people of yours are merely Vedic scholars; their intellect is destroyed by rote recitation and does not perceive subtle meanings. (MBh 12.10.1) By the phrase "destroyed by rote recitation," he refers even to the logical arguments of those who employ reasoning, because they are [merely] verbal and lack true existence. And furthermore, this other [point]:
"No one who follows the Smṛti should serve those Lokāyatika brāhmaṇas;

for these fools, who consider themselves wise, are skilled only in what is useless. By this [verse], the hearing of false reasoning is established, while by the preceding [verse], the permission of true reasoning is indicated; that indeed is "that" [the same thing].

Some assert that the Veda possesses authority because it was composed by God; yet such a possibility does not exist. Furthermore, on that view, the Veda would not be an authoritative means of knowledge, for in that case, God would merely be the one who establishes the linguistic convention (*samaya*).

When these [scriptures] are heard, an unauthoritative and erroneous adherence arises; therefore, they are merely fallacious reasoning (*asattarka*). Furthermore, they are of no use whatsoever for the comprehension of Vedic statements. Thus the Sāṃkhyas say: "For that [pleasure] is indeed characterized by impurity, decay, and excess" (SāṃK 2). Akṣapāda also considers them to be unauthoritative. And likewise, it was established in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the ritualists (*yājñika*) regarding what has been recited by someone: (NyāS 2.1.57).

The exposition of the *Karmamīmāṃsā* and *Vedānta* is understood according to the sacred revelation (*śruti*) as follows: "The gods went from this world to that world; the seers (*ṛṣis*) followed after them; men said to them, 'How then shall we exist? To them the seers imparted all ritual action (*sarvakarman*). According to this scripture, "Therefore, whatever the best of Brahmins reflect upon, that becomes the word of the seers (*ārṣa*). This [verse] restates the meaning of the aforementioned categories of reasoning (*tarka*). 12.106.
This action leading to the supreme good has been explained in its entirety; now the secret of this treatise of Manu is being taught. 12.107

This verse is intended to address the *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas) for the purpose of generating an intense longing for the meaning that is about to be explained. "Secret" (*rahasya*) means hidden; therefore, it must not be disclosed to everyone. It should not be revealed to one who is not intent on service, nor to one who has not attained supreme devotion, nor to one whose nature is not steadfast. (12.107)
If it should be asked how one should act regarding those dharmas not explicitly prescribed, whatever learned Brahmins may declare shall be the dharma, free from doubt. (12.108)

But surely, what doubt can there be regarding those things that have not been recorded? If it is argued, "I do not know how it would be in this case," [the response is] because that does not apply to them at all. It is said: what is intended here by "not recorded" is not such a thing; rather, it refers to that which is recorded in general, but whose specific details are not known.

But surely, even in that case, what is the doubt? Since a universal depends only upon its particulars, the purpose of the scripture is accomplished by any [particular] whatsoever; for example, regarding the rule "one should rinse with water," although waters are divided into various types such as those from wells, stagnant pools, or rivers, any of these being employed fulfill the purpose of the scripture.

True. Where there is a scriptural prohibition [351], but no specific expiation (*prāyaścitta*) has been taught, it is in such cases that this is prescribed. When a certain vessel containing the leavings of a Śūdra is impure, and because of contact with it becomes unclean—if someone should eat from it before it has been purified—then what is the expiation? Such is the doubt. For that inquiry ends in certainty, and through perception and other means, it is rightly established that it is indeed the leavings of a woman or a Śūdra; thus it ought to be considered as something not given. Indeed, it cannot be said that it is the leavings of a Śūdra. What does that have to do with its being his leavings? In cases of doubt such as these, the word of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) must be accepted as authority [353]. For example, when Śūdras and others are dependent on Brāhmaṇas, they have this doubt regarding Dharma. It is proper for them to act exactly as instructed by the learned. And therefore, whatever determination is made according to the degree of deficiency or excess, that alone is the Dharma in that case. There is no fault even for those who instruct them in such a manner. As it is said: "That shall be the Dharma, free from doubt. There is fault for one who speaks what is non-Dharma; but what hesitation can there be regarding Dharma? Likewise, when there is doubt regarding *gotra* and *pravara*, and the traditional codes (*smṛti*) have somehow been lost, the determination of *gotra* and *pravara* is achieved through the word of Brāhmaṇas. And in that regard, regarding doubt about the *pravara*, it is stated: "In the doubt 'Mānava for all'" (ĀśŚ 1.3.5). Well then, it will be the same for doubt regarding the *gotra*. But in that case, if there is no doubt about the *gotra*, how can there be doubt about the *pravara*, since the *pravaras* are recited differently for each *gotra*? This is indeed possible: the name of the *gotra* may be known, yet the *pravaras* are distinct and the *gotras* are manifold. Thus, even when there is certainty regarding the *pravara*, doubt regarding the *gotra* arises. || 12.108 ||
Those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been mastered according to the Dharma,
they are to be known as cultured Brahmins, the authorities for the Vedas and direct perception.
The definition of a cultured person (*śiṣṭa*) is stated by this [verse].
But is it not the case that the definition of a cultured person was already stated there in the passage, "Those who are unattached to wealth and pleasure" (MDh 2.13)?

Furthermore, another meaning for that term was suspected there; therefore, that passage does not have the definition as its sole purpose. And as for what Vasiṣṭha stated, "A cultured person, moreover, is one whose soul is free from desire" (VaDh 1.6), in that instance, learning (*vidvattā*) is not mentioned.
Because it is complete therein, that [Veda] has been realized in its meaning and understood; thus, it is accompanied by its supplements (*saparibṛṃhaṇa*). And so says your own Vyāsa:
"One should augment the meaning of the Veda by means of the *Itihāsas* and the *Purāṇas*."

The *smṛtis* (traditions) likewise have their objects thus established. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇas" is a restatement (*anuvāda*), because they alone have the authority to proclaim the Dharma. They have as their causes both revelation (*śruti*) and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Direct perception and causes constitute "direct-perception-causes. By the word "cause," the means of valid cognition other than direct perception are meant. Those for whom revelation, direct perception, and causes are [their authorities] are "those who have revelation, direct perception, and causes as their authorities. This is what is being said: just as direct perception possesses an indisputable validity, so too do they consider such a revelation to be authoritative; they place their trust even in those means of knowledge arising from causes (*hetūttha*), and they regard revelation itself as reasoning (*tarka*), yet they do not accept this [Dharma] as authoritative by relying on the science of logic (*hetuśāstra*).

Alternatively, *śruti* refers to direct revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*). The word "direct" (*pratyakṣa*) is applied to scriptural cognition because it is equivalent to direct perception. Those for whom that [scriptural authority] is the cause—the means—for the full understanding of dharma and adharma are described in this way. (12.109)
Whatever dharma an assembly of at least ten members may determine,
or even one of at least three who are established in virtuous conduct, that dharma shall not be overturned.

"Ten at the minimum" means that ten are the lowest number required; if more than ten are not available, ten must certainly be present. In their absence, there should be at least three. The phrase "as previously stated" refers to what was said in verse 2.13: "of those unattached to wealth and desire"—this is a restatement of that very point. Furthermore, this is not a count of persons, but rather a count of qualities (*guṇa*). Accordingly, he will say later: "even one who knows the Veda" (MDh 12.113). Since it is generally impossible for a single individual to possess the entire collection of such qualities, the enumeration is made by taking the person as the primary unit. (12.110)
He now shows those qualities which serve as the causes for a [worthy] assembly:

"One who possesses the threefold knowledge, one who knows the reasons, a logician, an etymologist, a reciter of the Dharma, and the three [members] of the preceding stages of life—such an assembly shall consist of at least ten members. (12.111)

Even though the description emphasizes the person (*puruṣapradhāna*), it should be understood as being subordinate to the qualities (*guṇaparataiva*). [376] One who is "versed in the three Vedas" (*traividya*) is a student of the three Vedas and a knower of their meaning. [377] He is "skilled in inference and so forth," that is, a logician (*tarkī*) endowed with the intellect capable of reasoning and refutation (*ūhāpoha*).

Now, it was indeed stated that for one who knows thus, the status of being a knower of the Vedic meaning is not even possible. True; however, even through the instruction of another, some degree of knowledge of the mere Vedic meaning—like a request—may still occur. Therefore, it is said that he "shines" by means of conviction (*pratyaya*) caused by the grasping of the Vedic meaning. [378–379]

By this, the etymological explanation is clarified. A *dharmapāṭhaka* is one who studies the legal treatises (*smṛti-śāstra*) of Manu and others. These three types of persons belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*) are indeed more proficient in the duties (*dharma*) when intent upon their performance. Some say they are the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), and the mendicant (*bhikṣu*), for his entry into the village is not prohibited. Furthermore, Gautama has recorded this sequence: "The student, the householder, the mendicant, and the forest-dweller" (GDh 3.2).
But others say: "Since there is no permission for violence, how could he resort to dharma? Therefore, one should go into the presence of the ascetic together with others. 12.111.

One who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and likewise one who knows the Sāmaveda—this assembly of at least three is to be known as the authority for resolving doubts regarding dharma. (12.112)

The meaning of the Vedas is understood through etymology (nirukta), grammar (vyākaraṇa), and hermeneutics (mīmāṃsā). And all of these are common [to all the Vedas]. For it is not the case that the meaning of one Veda is understood there but not that of another; this method is eternal. Now, how is the distinction between the Ṛgveda and so forth established? Likewise, regarding this, it has been stated there according to the differences among the Gṛhyasūtras: 12.112.

Even if he is alone, whatever dharma a preeminent twice-born man who knows the Vedas determines should be known as the supreme dharma; it is not [dharma] proclaimed by tens of thousands of the ignorant.

"Should resolve" means that having reached a certainty, one should speak; even if uttered by tens of thousands of ignorant fools, [the answer] is explained first [in the following verse]. || 12.113 ||
For those who lack vows, who lack mantras, and who subsist on mere birth—even if they have gathered by the thousands—no true assembly exists. (12.114)

The meaning already stated previously regarding "those who do not observe vows" is here expressed by way of contrast. Whatever resolution those who observe vows—those who study the Vedas—declare, therein neither the learned nor the unlearned should entertain doubt. For this very reason, no light-minded assumption should be made, treating it as if it were equivalent to a mere quality. (12.114)
Whatever those who are shrouded in darkness, the foolish who do not know the Dharma, declare to be the Dharma—that sin becomes a hundredfold and follows after those who spoke it. (12.115)
The statement of faults regarding ignorant speakers. 12.115.
All this has been declared to you, which brings about the supreme good;
a Brahmin who does not fall away from this attains the highest goal.

This verse [MDh 1.109] constitutes the summary of the dharma that was promised. Regarding what was asked in the words, “You ought to tell us the dharmas” (MDh 1.2), and what was promised as the subject to be spoken in the words, “O great sages, let it be heard” (MDh 1.4)—all of that has now been told; thus he declares the completion of the treatise (*śāstra*). But surely there is more of the treatise that follows, such as the section on those who must be killed and so forth, which is heard as being enjoined by injunction (*vidhi*). Since that portion falls within the scope of injunction, how can it be said that the treatise is concluded? Generally, a speaker does not provide a summary until the very end.

Furthermore, since knowledge is taught as being independent and purely pure once the remainder of ritual action has been transcended, there is no contradiction. The purpose of stating the conclusion by declaring that knowledge—characterized by the dharma which is the goal of the scriptures—is superior in all respects, is as follows: [verse 12.116].
Thus that Blessed Lord, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
has told me all this, the supreme secret of the Dharma.

"Bhṛgu said to his disciples: 'That Blessed One, Manu, has proclaimed this entire treatise for the welfare of the world. By this, the desire for further authority is dispelled. Whatever is secret concerning the inner self (*adhyātma*), that too Manu revealed after instructing me; and by me, it has been made manifest to you according to tradition. Thus, there is no need for further desire for action. (12.117)
One who is composed should perceive everything—both the existent and the non-existent—within the self;
for by perceiving everything within the self, one does not direct the mind toward unrighteousness. (12.118)

The entire world, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, is subject to the nature of arising and destruction. Now, one should perceive everything—whether non-existent like a hare's horn or existent and eternal like space—as established within the Self; thus, one should meditate upon it as abiding in the Self.

The object of seeing—that is, the clear object—is known through meditation (*upāsanā*) that culminates in direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*). Indeed, direct realization cannot occur through a single instance of seeing; thus the esoteric scripture (*rahasya-śāstra*) teaches it in this way. In that context, regarding the meditation on the Self, it is said: "It is to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.4.5). Thus, true seeing culminates in meditation. Meditation on the Self is defined as the practice of knowledge as taught, uninterrupted by heterogeneous cognitions. Alternatively, the necessity of practice is implied by the force of the context, because purificatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*) fulfill their own purpose by imparting a specific quality to the object to be purified. For example, in the injunction "One threshes the rice grains" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 1.21.7), the unstated [purpose] is introduced; for if it were seen merely for its own sake, it would have an invisible result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and being a ritual injunction, it would lose its status as a purificatory act. Therefore, the phrase "one should see" should be understood as declaring the culmination in that single object of knowledge, by excluding knowledge whose objects are other things to be known.

Regarding this, they dispute over the term *ātman*. What indeed is this so-called *ātman*? If it were the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) whose locus is the body, then the subsequent statement, "the ruler, golden-hued" (MDh 12.122), would be contradicted. For the birth of the body—which is subject to action—from death is not heard [in scripture]; rather, it is said: "Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart" (BĀU 3.8.9). Therefore, the rule of transmigratory existence does not apply even to the *ātman* that is the object of the notion of "I. Hence, some other proof of its essential nature must be stated. Furthermore, this being the case, by means of the injunction "one should see," there is a subsumption (*upasaṃhāra*) of external selves—those established as the *ādhibhautika* and *ādhidaivika*—into the *ādhyātmika* state. And the scriptural *atarāga* (non-attachment) remains as a means; it attains a connection with that which has been acquired through the causal self.

Now, as for the statement that one should always perceive within oneself the entire world as delimited by the causal Puruṣa—therein it must be explained what kind of perception of the Self is meant "within the Self.

Others, however, think that this arrangement is appropriate only for the embodied self (*śarīrātman*); for it is logical that its possession of those qualities [of the world] occurs through its identification with the hearer.

To this it is replied: First of all, the word *ātman* has been established as referring to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) by the authority of other scriptural passages with which it is consistent. As for the objection that its essential nature (*svarūpa*) must be explained, what else could possibly be said beyond this injunction regarding its being a hearer and a knower? Those passages are to be understood from every Upaniṣad across all the Vedic branches (*śākhās*). Since even other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are devoted solely to establishing oneness, the effort expended by the Mīmāṃsakas against perception (*pratyakṣa*), which grasps [this unity], is indeed in vain. And it has been stated in the *Vākyapadīya*: "There is no such thing as that which is not included in the name," and so forth. Furthermore, the fact that [the Self] is to be understood through injunction is to be inferred from its being concealed by the body.

As for what was said—"How can that which is non-existent be seen?"—the meaning of this is "existent and non-existent. "Existent" is a designation for the aggregate of transformations (*vikāragrāma*); "non-existent" refers to its very imperceptibility due to its subtlety, which makes it impossible to determine [as a discrete entity].

Furthermore, as for what was said—"There is no connection of the Supreme Self with the ear"—what here is connected? [The answer is] everything, because He has been established as the cause of the maintenance, origination, and destruction of the entire world.

And as for this method of arrangement, its meaning is this: whatever appears as differentiated, all that one should dissolve into non-duality; "everything is situated in the Self"—this is the reason found for the general cessation [of duality] from the Supreme Self.

"Concentrated. The meaning is that "concentration" (samādhi) is the means for the cessation of mental fluctuations, which should be learned from the Yoga scriptures. One does not direct the mind toward unrighteousness; rather, there is a state of immobility of both the intellect and the consciousness. One should practice until the mind is no longer carried away by disputants; and therefore, one should dissolve whatever causes distraction. (12.118)
The self alone is all the deities; everything is established within the self.
For the self indeed produces the connection with action for these embodied beings.

In all cases, sacrificial acts such as the *yāga* and so forth, as well as the heavens and the deities, are to be viewed as the Self. This very deity Agni is none other than the Self; there is no deity Agni apart from that. Thus it has been said: "The one Self is heard of in many ways" (*Nirukta* 7.4). Where it is joined [with the mantra]: "I am indeed the one Self, the deity" (*Ṛgveda* 1.164.46); likewise, "They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni; the wise speak of the One Being in many ways" (*Ṛgveda* 1.164.46)—by this [passage], which states that those who see a deity other than the Supreme Self of manifold forms "fall away from existence," the viewing of the deities who are parts of the ritual as the Self is enjoined.
What then? He has no need for the ritual service of deities and so forth; all accomplishment comes through his very selfhood alone. How so?
"It does not produce them within its own nature as an object.
In the application of action, there is a connection between the action and its fruit; that self of theirs brings it about. It is no other deity, nor is it possessed of those qualities. || 12.119 ||
One should place the ether within the cavities, the wind within movement and touch,
the supreme fire within digestion and sight, the waters within moisture, and the earth within solid forms.

One should restrain the external space within these nine apertures; that [space] is indeed the external space, for there is nothing external whatsoever. "Anila" means wind; one should settle it there. There is a certain bodily state characterized by the movement and vibration of the hands, feet, and so forth, as well as touch characterized by the external and other qualities; one should settle the wind there. Digestion is produced by the gastric fire (*jaṭharāgni*), as is vision; one should settle those two there. "Tejas" (fire) is the supreme [element], black, abiding in the form of the sun; one should settle it in the moisture consisting of fat, marrow, and so on—this is understood from the context. "Gām" means the earth; one should settle it in the "mūrtis," which are the parts of the body. (12.120)

Thus is the withdrawal of the great elements. Now, the installation of the deities will be described: one should place the Moon in the mind, the Quarters in the ears, Viṣṇu in the stride, Hara in strength, Agni in speech, Mitra in excretion, and Prajāpati in procreation. (12.121)

One should establish in the mind this very moon, Indu; it is not the moon that moves through the sky, but rather that which is situated in my mind. And as for the quarters [of space], they reside within the power of the sense of hearing. When one who strides even a little distance anywhere, Viṣṇu alone is established there by the act of striding (*krānti*). Likewise, [one should see] Hara in strength (*bala*). The swift rising of the jaw is the domain of the senses, having the form of time; it is indeed the activity of the senses. One should view this emission of the fire of speech through the mantras beginning with Vāyu. Having thus withdrawn everything into the self, one should perceive it all in the Supreme Self. Such is the cause established in the Supreme Self: "I am nothing other than That. In this manner, this entire worship should be performed. (12.121)
One should know that Supreme Person as the ruler of all, subtler even than the subtle, radiant like gold, and attainable through the intellect in deep sleep. 12.122.

He says this very thing: [the Lord is] the ruler, the controller of all beings from the Brāhmaṇas down to the Śūdras. That which is the fixed nature of heat and so forth in fire and other elements; that which is the supreme, internal power of the sun and other luminaries; that which is the activity of revolving and illuminating the world; and that which is the specific determination of the fruits of actions—all that exists because of that Controller. As it has been said: "Under the command of this very Imperishable, O Gārgī," and likewise: "The sun shines, and the moon rains... [and so on].

"Out of fear, fire and wind, and death as the fifth, run [after him]" (KaṭU 6.3). Thus, regarding the phrase "smaller even than the small": if anyone were to claim that the wife's size is a third part of the measure of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair and so forth, that would be establishing an unreal dimension; for there is a negation of all attributes in such passages as "neither gross nor subtle" (BṛU 3.8.8). What then? It is because she is to be understood by a mind as sharp as the tip of a blade of kuśa grass. This is what is meant: one who is not extremely skillful, nor yet habituated to such practice. (12.122)
Some call him Agni, others Manu, others Prajāpati; some call him Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman. (12.123)
Pervading all beings with his five forms,
he perpetually causes them to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay.
Thus, he who perceives the Self within all beings by means of his own self, having attained equanimity toward all, reaches Brahman, the supreme state. (12.125)

"Becoming Brahman" means attaining the state of Brahman. By the manifestation of friendliness and other virtues, he describes the destruction of passion and hatred. And by this, he states that the knowledge of the oneness of the Self, uninterrupted by heterogeneous cognitions, must be practiced; for when heterogeneous cognitions arise, universal consensus is not achieved. Therefore, this is what is meant: for one who has abandoned the notions of "I" and "mine," Brahman—in the form of unsurpassed supreme bliss—is attained through the necessity of that singular knowledge. The cessation of the undesirable and the attainment of the intended goal as demonstrated by the scriptures constitute the accomplishment of the fruit; such is the meaning. (12.123–25)
Thus, by reciting this Mānava Śāstra proclaimed by Bhṛgu, a twice-born man becomes constantly possessed of right conduct and shall attain his desired goal.

The word *iti* indicates the completion of the treatise. By reciting it, one becomes possessed of right conduct (*ācāravān*). Another aspect of conduct is to be supplied: namely, the practical application of the treatise according to how it has been studied. If one is of such a nature, one attains the desired goal characterized by the deities and so forth. (12.126)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
The *Manusmṛti* is indeed venerable, yet Medhātithi’s appropriate commentary upon it has been lost due to the power of fate, such that no manuscript can be found anywhere.
King Madana, together with his son Araṇasuta, had [the work] brought from another land.
He then undertook the restoration of the worn-out [text] by having copies of those manuscripts written here and there.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the Commentary on Manu, composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
